maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. L. RALSTON

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to say a few words as president of the Canadian Bar Association about a man who was not only a pillar of the Bar Association, but one of its rarest ornaments.
Canadian lawyers are proud to claim the late Colonel Ralston as one of their very own. They mourn his death and will long cherish the example he has set to his profession in the various avenues of their high calling.
Perhaps I may be permitted to say here in part what I have said elsewhere about Colonel Ralston and his sudden and much lamented death.
Colonel James Layton Ralston died at the end of the day,-a day like all his days, filled with labour. He led a life of labour.

Tribute to the late Hon. J. L. Ralston
Well equipped physically and mentally, he turned to account every ounce of energy that his stout frame and powerful intellect were capable of generating. Few men in our time have successfully engaged in broader fields of endeavour; none has been more unsparing of self.
Ralston was in turn lawyer, soldier and politician.	In each of these callings he
excelled; in each he left enduring marks and abiding friendships; in all, his way was lit by the lamps of a purpose that never wavered, of a courage that never weakened, and of ideals that never dimmed.	Ralston was
primarily and always a lawyer. In early manhood as his first choice he went to the law; to the law he returned from both soldiering and politics. He was admitted to the Nova Scotia bar at the early age of twenty-one, and to the Quebec bar half-way through his career.
His capacious mind and its easy intake, his faithful and well-stored memory, his intellectual curiosity, his gift of orderly and lucid exposition, his endless industry, made of him one of the great Canadian advocates of his generation. He understood the meaning of professional duty in its public no less than in its private aspects. He was alive to the traditions of the Bar. He knew that it has functions of supreme importance to the life of a free country, that its members are called upon to develop and exercise qualities of leadership and guidance which are not exacted from the members of any other profession. He knew that in a democracy where all are subject to the law, and where so much depends upon the interplay of political parties for the enactment of good laws and their fair administration, the lawyer is better qualified than many to make a contribution to public life, and his he made generous, wholesome and vigorous.
He suffered the fortune and the fate of those engaged in the endless adventure of governing men-no more, no less. Ralston understood. He did not complain. He considered it a privilege to have given of his best in field and forum to the public service of his country. When this came to an end he returned to his briefs, not sad and dejected, but lighthearted and joyous. He had done his duty; he had retained his ideals; he had kept his friends.
To live in hearts we leave behind
Is not to die.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. L. RALSTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have naturally, knowing there would be those who, like myself, would wish to make reference to the
late Colonel Ralston, given careful thought to what should be said or done in the house this afternoon regarding the passing of one of the greatest public servants Canada has had.
Part of my duty as leader of the house and Prime Minister is to preserve traditional practice and to be careful in the matter of establishing precedent. I therefore had a careful search made as to what had taken place in parliament in the past, and have been unable to find that at any time, with one exception only, has reference been made by the leaders of the parties to the passing of former members of governments who were not members of the parliament then in session. The only exception, so far as I have been able to ascertain, has been with former prime ministers or leaders of political parties. I considered whether it would be proper for me to depart from the traditional practice today, or rather to set a precedent which it might become embarrassing to follow in some future cases. Before taking my seat this afternoon I had a word with the acting leader of the opposition and mentioned to him that I did not think, for the reasons I have mentioned, that I should depart from what has been the customary practice and thereby establish a new precedent.
However, I am happy indeed that the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) as president of the Canadian Bar Association, has found the best of reasons for drawing the attention of the house to the loss which the legal profession of this country has suffered in the passing of the late Colonel Ralston. May I say that I echo sincerely and deeply all the sentiments that he has expressed. I would say on behalf of the public of Canada that I think Canada has lost one of the finest men of our country in the passing of the late Colonel Ralston.
I knew Colonel Ralston intimately, and a more unselfish and self-sacrificing public servant I have never known. I cannot recall anyone of my acquaintance who seemed to be more industrious, more conscientious or more ready to sacrifice everything for duty, as he saw it, than Colonel Ralston. We had our difference as to what was the most advisable course to be adopted at a particular time, but such differences arise in government and are sometimes inevitable. As far as I am aware, that difference, which was a political difference, did not make a difference in our personal friendship. I continued to retain to the end of his life the strongest affection for Colonel Ralston and the greatest possible admiration for his high character and exceptional abilities. I believe that the great service which he rendered our country in the period of the war

years as Minister of National Defence brought *a reaction which was inevitable. I would think that it helped to account for the shortening of his life. But those wrho knew Colonel Ralston will realize with me that he was a man who [DOT]could not spare himself no matter what particular task he might be engaged in. As has been reported in the press, he was apparently following his customary habit of working until half past six or seven o'clock at night before returning from his duties to his evening meal. I would not have been surprised if the evening had found him engaged again on the task he had in hand. Certainly it was so through the years that he was here as Minister of National Defence'. The continual taxing of his energies, and what must frequently have been the overtaxing of his strength undoubtedly contributed to his sudden passing at the age of sixty-six. I feel that our own country is very greatly the loser in the death of one who held so high a place in his profession, who played so important a part in public life, and who took such a great part in the larger task of helping to save the world's freedom when freedom itself was at stake.
I do not think we should ever forget that Colonel Ralston, when the first war came on. gave up his practice to join Canada's armed forces for service overseas, and that his was a heroic part. He served with great distinction through the whole of the first war. When a second war threatened, I remember talking with him very earnestly before w'ar actually broke out. Fearing that something of the kind might happen, I begged of him to come into the ministry forthwith. He told me in his quiet, humble, modest way that he had felt the need of making provision for his family and himself and for that reason did not wish to come back into the government, but that if war came I could call on him in a moment. When war came, I asked him again to come into the government, and he responded instantly. No one could have rendered the country greater service in the time that he was minister of the department of defence than Colonel Ralston. His name will always be greatly honoured in this country, and nowhere more than in this parliament, and by none more than by those who knew him best.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. L. RALSTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as an old personal friend of Colonel Ralston, a fellow Nova Scotian, and also as the honorary head of the Canadian Bar Association, I should like to add a brief and simple tribute to the great man whose death has just occurred.
Colonel Ralston never did a selfish thing in his whole life, and I cannot think of anyone whose death would cause more widespread

sorrow than his. A truly great Canadian has passed away, and his countless friends are shocked and grieving. His whole life was devoid of selfishness and filled with distinction. A brave soldier, a fine lawyer, a wise statesman, he brought honour and glory to Canada throughout his whole illustrious career. His devotion to duty, his intellectual honesty, his frankness and courage, his capacity for self sacrifice, his unfailing manliness in all the activities and relationships of life, were altogether exceptional. His heart was full of human sympathy, his friendships were innumerable, his loyalty to old comrades and friends unshakeable.
To his devoted wife and son I extend my deepest sympathy.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. L. RALSTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who had the privilege of sitting in. this house with Colonel Ralston when he sat on this side, and also when he was a member of the government, I wish to associate myself and the C.C.F. group with the tributes paid to his memory by the member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley).
I shall remember Colonel Ralston best because of the meticulous care with which he answered, or at least attempted to answer, every letter L wrote him during the time he occupied the position of minister of defence. I knew how busy he was, and how many important questions he had to deal with, and I refrained whenever possible from writing him in regard to anything. But as happens with all private members, I had occasion, at times, to put questions to him, and no matter how much trouble the answer involved I always got an answer which was full and complete in every detail. I am sure that that is the way in which he will be remembered by most of the members, at least on this side of the house.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. L. RALSTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as the member for Peace River (Mr. Low) was not a member of parliament while Colonel Ralston was winning the admiration of the whole house by his estimable behaviour in the cabinet during wartime, he has asked me to say a word on behalf of the Social Credit group.
After all the beautiful and noble things that have been said, it seems utterly impossible for me to say anything more, or to say it any better. But an inspiring passage referring to the war comes to my mind at this moment, as put into the mouth of a soldier boy who was called upon to make the supreme sacrifice. The words are, "Now, God be thanked, Who has

Tribute to the late Hon. J. L. Ralston
matched us with His hour." I believe those words are exceedingly appropriate as applied to Colonel Ralston. In his spiritual life, having left this life of storm and stress, he must now be able to say with great satisfaction, "Now, God be thanked, Who has matched us with His hour."
The members of my group join with all other members of the house in deep appreciation of Colonel Ralston's fine life, and in tenderest sympathy and good will toward his bereaved ones.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. L. RALSTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that as the member for Prince, the constituency represented in this house from 1939 to 1945 by the late Colonel Ralston, I should add a few words to what has been already said by the other speakers.
I believe that I am voicing the feelings of every one of my constituents and the people of the maritimes in general, regardless of politics, race or creed, when I say that in the passing of the late Colonel Ralston the maritimes have lost one of their most distinguished sons. Colonel Ralston had a tremendous capacity for forming deep and abiding friendships. During the six years he represented . Prince he made many such friendships. I well recall that on a return from a trip to the battlefronts in Italy, Colonel Ralston spent literally hours telephoning the friends and relatives of boys he had met and talked to while overseas. Such genuine acts of courtesy and thoughtfulness on the part of a busy man are not soon forgotten.
On behalf of my constituents and myself, I wish to express deepest sympathy to the family of the late Colonel Ralston.

maintopic: THE LATE HON. J. L. RALSTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to associate the Progressive Conservative party, of which I have the honour at the moment to be the acting leader, with the sentiments which have been so eloquently expressed by those who have preceded me.
I felt when I heard the news of Colonel Ralston's death that it was almost like losing a member of one's own family; for through the war years he had endeared himself to all of us who sat with him in parliament and had anything to do with his department. His courtesy, his friendliness, and, as one hon. member has said, his capacity to hold his friends, singled him out and made him one of the very great men with whom we have had the honour to associate. His courage, his brilliance, his almost indefatigable attention to every detail of the duties at hand, and his devotion to that duty, marked him in the hearts, minds and memories of all of us as one of nature's gentlemen. No greater tribute than that can one man pay to another.
On behalf of the party with which I am associated, Mr. Speaker, I join with other hon. members who have spoken, in conveying to the late Colonel Ralston's widow, and to his son, deep and genuine sympathy in this their hour of sorrow and of loss.

speechtext:
This is the place to introduce a new clause, according to Beauchesne, 670 and 671. I need not speak at great length on the amendment I shall now propose to section 406, because I covered that when I spoke on the second reading of the bill. The minister has informed me that there will be a number of special amendments next year to those parts of the Canada Shipping Act relating to the technical end of radiotelegraphy. My amendment is not a technical one, being intended rather to ensure safety, and there is no need for any technical knowledge to understand the meaning of it.
Section 406 of the Canada Shipping Act is the section that stipulates what type of ship shall carry radiotelegraph operators as a safety measure. Subsection 1 satisfactorily covers deep-sea ships and cargo ships. Section 406 (2) is the section referring to coastal steamers plying on the east and west coasts. The intent of the act is a good one. The section states that a ship certified to carry 50 or more persons shall have a radio operator if it makes a voyage of more than 200 nautical miles from place to place. The second subsection states that the bigger ships carrying 250 persons must have an operator if they make voyages of more than 90 miles from place to place, and the third subsection provides that if they carry 500 passengers or more they may go only twenty miles from place to place without such an operator.
When this act was drawn up I am quite sure it was intended to cover the situation I shall describe. Another section of the act to which I call attention shows the great importance which is attached to proper radiotelegraph service at sea. Section 40 gives the minister amazing powers. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) commented on the wide powers given the minister in case of emergency. He can allow ships to go to sea without a certified captain or deck officers or engineer officers, without steamship inspectors or proper loading; but there is one significant subsection of this clause which provides that while he can do all these things, he cannot allow any leeway in relation to those aspects that concern radiotelegraph installations on ships.
This is not only important as far as the people who drew the act are concerned; it is extremely important to the people of British Columbia. As I pointed out in my earlier remarks, our province has a very heavy coastal steamer traffic north and south. Our coast, while picturesque, is a dangerous and treacherous one to navigate, especially in the winter, when unfortunately we have not only heavy
Canada Shipping Act

rains but dense fog. Moreover, our coast is a very badly lighted one. We have not one quarter of the aids to navigation on the British Columbia coast, in the way of lights, buoys, foghorns and so on, that the Americans have, either on the coast of the United States itself or on the coast of Alaska.
It has been mentioned also by the British Columbia members that we have not a coastguard to help in rescue work on the British Columbia coast as have the Americans. For these reasons the people of British Columbia are anxious that the coastal steamer traffic shall be properly protected by adequate radiotelegraph service.
Unfortunately, while the intent of the act is good, there have been infringements and evasions-not, I am glad to say, by the two major steamship lines, Canadian Pacific Steamships and Canadian National Steamships, but by some of the smaller lines which ply the coast. They have taken advantage of.the fact that in the act the length of journey is defined as "from place to place," and therefore the coastal steamers can make the voyage of 500 miles to Prince Rupert, along all that hazardous coast carrying 400 passengers, and evade -the stipulations of the act by merely calling every 90 miles at some small fishing cannery, logging camp or paper town. Such places could not give to a ship in distress the service which is expected. The reason for limiting the voyages of ships of this type is that if the ship is in distress, aid in the way of salvage tugs, high speed tugs and medical help can be sent to points which the ship had left or towards which it was headed; and above all, that these points should have wireless listening posts at which someone will be listening for distress calls, and to which the coastal steamer could send a call if it is in distress. Such posts are not found in these little logging towns, which are used as "places" under the act. They have none of these facilities. They have no tugs or lifeboats which could go out to give aid. They have no medical aid at hand. Seldom have they a doctor. As they have no listening posts, a ship could be in distress five miles away and nobody in these little towns would be any the wiser.
The people of British Columbia, therefore, have indicated strongly that they think this act should be strengthened. The weakness arises from the words "place to place". It has been suggested that we use the terminology which is used in the United Kingdom with regard to coastal traffic, namely, "terminus to terminus". This, however, might apply to a ship, for example,, going from Vancouver to Alaska, passing two or three points en route which are places from which aid could go out.

Public opinion at home has pretty well decided that "public harbour to public harbour" is a much better definition than "place to place", a public harbour being a place designated under this act, the Canada Shipping Act. Every public harbour has a harbour master, and from these harbours you could expect aid in the way of tugs or lifeboats, and medical aid; and there would be maintained at each of them a listening post.
I should like to refer the minister, if he is at all in doubt as to the opinion in our province, to the feeling expressed last winter in editorials in all the papers after we had a fatal wreck on one of our small coastal steamers. Only last week two papers in British Columbia which consistently support this government, the Vancouver Sun and the Victoria Daily Times, both carried long editorials on the subject, one entitled "Safety on the coast", and the other "Safety at sea".
If the minister wants other proof, I am sure the hon. member for Yukon, who during the fifty years he has been active in the west has probably travelled our British Columbia coast more than any other member in this house, or the hon. member for Vancouver East, or the hon. member for Kootenay East, can support me in this contention.
I do not think that I can say anything further, so I will now move my amendment, which is as follows:
That section 406 2(a) of the Canada Shipping Act be amended by substituting in subparagraphs (i), (ii) and (iii) the phrase from "public harbour to public harbour" w'herever the phrase "place to place" now occurs.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
I rise only to support this amendment. I know that greater safety is required than is at present provided by the regulations affecting ships plying on the Pacific coast. I understand that some of the opposition to providing radiotelegraph on the ships, an operator for that purpose, arises out of the small amount of work the person in charge would have to do. I submit that is not a good argument. If it were a good argument, instead of having full-time firemen in our cities, who may be on duty for weeks without being called to a fire, we would have part-time firemen. The need for a radio operator on a ship is when an accident occurs, either to the ship which is so equipped, or to some other ship. It is a question of radiotelegraphy not only from ship to shore but also from ship to ship. The importance that is attributed to radiotelegraphy in the schedule to the safety at sea convention is a good indication of the value attached to it. There are over six pages of regulations. I suggest

Canada Shipping Act
that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver North is necessary at this time, and is especially necessary on the rugged coast of British Columbia where we have no coastguard service.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver North has clearly and completely stated the case for his proposed amendment. The act as it stands now, with the use of the word "place" in the various paragraphs, enables the steamship companies whose ships are not equipped with radiotelegraph to evade the act. They can have a short voyage from place to place, including a number of "places", on a whole long voyage; whereas if the words "public harbour" are substituted for the word "place" they cannot do that. As the hon. member for Vancouver North has said, the largest shipping companies on the west coast are properly equipped. I have been on these ships when they had to call for help. I have been on ships when other ships called them for help. If it had not been for the radiotelegraph, they would not have known that a ship was in trouble, nor could they have made their own needs known to the people on shore or to other ships. speechtext: Under the present provisions of the act, a C.P.R. steamer operating on the west of Vancouver island could get by the present provisions without providing a radio operator. I appreciate the fact that in the near future there will be extensive advances in the field of communication from ship to shore and from ship to ship. But if within the next few years a tragic accident should occur, even although radiotelegraph facilities might not have averted it, I suggest to the minister that he and his department would be in a much happier position, having regard to public opinion, if this amendment were allowed to pass.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have looked carefully at the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver North. While there is some merit in the proposal, I must oppose it, for the following reasons.
It has already been stated by myself during the course of this discussion that the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act were given careful consideration by a special committee
set up in the Department of Transport. It was a committee of experts and heads of various branches having jurisdiction over certain parts of the act. The committee heard representations from various associations, unions and groups across Canada. One of these associations was the commercial telegraphers union, Marconi section. They presented a brief having to do with amendments to the act in connection with radio, radiotelegraphy and the like, and there was no such representation as that which has been brought forward at this time.
There is sitting at the present time in London an international convention known as the convention for the safety of life at sea. That convention is considering amendments to the radio sections of the Canada Shipping Act, as well as to the safety sections of the act. Canada is one of the representative nations at the convention, and in all probability will be a signatory to it. I would hesitate to recommend amendments to the act when I do not know the recommendations to which in all probability Canada will be committed. I believe it is more in accordance with practice, and certainly with custom, to wait until those recommendations have been agreed upon. It may be that they will contain an amendment such as the one now suggested. It may be that there will be a complete revamping of the section. Until I am in possession of those recommendations I would hesitate to accept this amendment.
There is another reason which should be given consideration, and that is that the amendment has the tendency of materially strengthening the act. I presume there could be no complaint about that, other than the fact that there is a group of owners of certain vessels which are not equipped with radio apparatus and equipment; and it might very well be that this would work a hardship upon those people. I believe they have the right to expect that until the recommendations of the convention for the safety of life at sea have been brought in, no changes which would materially affect them, such as the amendment now offered, should be made. For those reasons I feel I should oppose the amendment.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
With all due deference to the minister, I suggest the answer he has given does not answer the point at all. I do not know why we should wait for the recommendations of an international convention before strengthening our own act so far as the coast of British Columbia is concerned. I have mentioned that the present word "place" would apply to little fishing
Canada Shipping Act

towns such as Lund, Egmont and Alert bay, and this should be sufficient to end the controversy.
To say that some international convention may bring in other regulations is not enough. I admit that some companies might be forced to install radio apparatus; but I should think we ought to consider the hardship which might befall two or three hundred passengers on a ship who may be facing a watery grave, and not the hardship to shipowners. The small cost of installing radiotelegraphy sets on these ships, as is done on Canadian National and Canadian Pacific ships, should not be considered as an obstacle.
For these reasons I suggest we should have a division on this matter.
Mr. MacINNIS' May I say another word before the amendment is voted on. My opinion is that the minister's argument as to why he cannot accept the amendment is so weak that it would have been better left unsaid.

The minister may, if he thinks fit, and upon such conditions, if any, as he thinks proper to impose, exempt any ship from any requirement contained in sections one hundred and thirteen, one hundred and fourteen, one hundred and thirty-two and one hundred and thirty-three, or dispense with the observance of any such requirements in the case of any ship, if he is satisfied that that requirement has been substantially complied with in the case of that ship, or that compliance with the requirement is unnecessary in the circumstances of the ease, and that the action taken or provision made as respects the subject matter of the requirement in the case of the ship is as effective as actual compliance with the requirement.
Section 40 is-

I would point out to the house that those two sections are a challenge not only to law and order but to the basic traditions of our political system and to the supremacy of the law and of parliamentary government. In effect, they state that what is now the law ceases to be the law if some individual decrees that it shall not be the law. It is an attack upon the rule of law and it is a perversion of parliamentary' government. It as an echo of the bill that was passed earlier this session, the act respecting the conservation of foreign exchange, when the minister in charge of that bill was given powers that enabled him to legislate for the country at large and to determine that laws in force had ceased to be effective.
In this case there is not even the alleged reason of urgency. We have listened to arguments advanced in support of legislation which has been brought forward in the house resting upon a doctrine of urgency or emergency. That doctrine, for the time being, was seriously challenged the other day by a judgment of a court which held, that, no emergency having been established, the legislation was entirely beyond the competence of parliament to enact.

Canada Shipping Act

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: But there is urgency here.

I challenge that statement. There has been no evidence of urgency and much less of emergency. It has been stated that it would be more convenient if the officers of the department over which the minister presides were permitted to deal rather summarily with situations which heretofore came under the law. I refer now to section 40.
Section 40 says in substance that the seventh part of the Merchant Shipping Act shall not apply whenever the minister, on the recommendation of the chairman of the board of steamship inspection, so decrees.
The board of steamship inspection is a creature of the minister and is in all probability comprised of gentlemen who are in the service of his department. I shall be glad to be corrected on this point if I am in error, because I have not yet been able to ascertain exactly who constitutes this board of steamship inspection, but I have noticed that its members are appointed by order in council, and it is fair to assume that they would in most cases be in complete harmony with the government and in all likelihood under the dominion and instructions of the minister.
Let us look for a moment at the seventh part of the shipping act. It deals with many aspects of shipping, and it deals with those questions which affect humanity most, that is the safety of those who go down to the sea in ships. In fact, the whole seventh part comes under the general heading of "safety". It includes in the act fifty odd pages of the statute and it consists of something like 125 sections-116 sections to be exact.
If this bill becomes law it will mean that that entire seventh part of the Canada Shipping Act will cease to have the effect of law and may be suspended, deleted, changed or otherwise dealt with as the minister sees fit, without notice and without reason.
Among the items which may be dealt with in this summary way are the following: steamship inspection service; safety and inspection certificates; provisions as to safety convention ships not registered in Canada; limited and other voyages; overloading passenger ships; safety precautions; radio equipment; inspection of radiotelegraph apparatus; radio certificates; load lines and loading; special provisions to load line convention ships not registered in Canada; general provisions to loadline convention ships not registered in Canada; loading of timber; changes affecting certificate; safety of ships, passengers and
crew; dangerous goods; ships alleged to be unseaworthy; inspection of ships' tackle; gangways and dock lines; exceptional vessels and exemptions from inspection; fees for inspection; detaining for non-compliance or other causes; discretionary application of safety of load line conventions, sale of ship to realize fines imposed; disposal of penalties and limitations of proceedings; general penalty; special application of this part.
This broad realm of shipping legislation in which, as the result of centuries of experience, these provisions have been embodied, first, in the British act and, subsequently, in our own act, shall cease to have the effect of law and be binding upon the people at large only so long as it meets with the approval of the minister. The minister, in making his statement to the house with regard to section 11, said that a similar provision is found in the British act and he suggested that was the reason to introduce such a measure into the Canada Shipping Act. I draw to his attention that, while the language of the British act does not differ materially from that of the Canadian act, there is this great difference: Whereas in the Canadian act discretion is left with the minister, under the Merchant Shipping Act of the United Kingdom the discretion rests with the board of trade.
I do not think it is necessary at the present time to enter into a lengthy discussion of the origin and function of the board of trade or the part which it plays in England. It is one of those hoary institutions that go back almost to the time King Canute. It is one of those institutions that has grown up in that seafaring country. It is associated in the minds of many with Trinity House, Deptford shipbuilding yards and other like agencies which were the product of initiative, enterprise and experience that sent Englishmen to the seven seas. They were not administered by civil servants or by persons who found themselves in relation to authority in the position that our departmental officials find themselves here. They lived on the banks of the Thames, in that harbour of ten thousand masts, and saw its commerce and trade pulsating day by day. They were of the life, of the essence of that great humanizing and colonizing agency that, through the centuries, made of Britain what she has been and is. To liken the minister- who, with all his grace and charm is but a passing phase on the political scene-to an institution that has been in existence for five, six, or seven hundred years is, I think, to show a lack of sense of proportion.
We pride ourselves on living in a country which acknowledges the rule of law, a country
Canada Shipping Act

in which everyone is subject to the law, and is supposed to know the law and is dealt with as if he knew the law. Yet under these amendments, under sections 11 and 40 of the bill, the law may be changed without notice and without reason at any time.
My hon. and genial friend, the minister of the department, said there is urgency. What urgency is there? This law has been the law since 1934 and it embodies enactments which were the law in Canada for a great many years before that. The laws which are affected by section 11 have to do with the certification of masters, mates and engineers, and the qualifications of men who are operating ships; it is important to the people who ply the trade of sailors and seamen and to the people who journey by sea, that there should be the utmost confidence and reliability at all times in those to whom they confide their lives every time they put out to sea. Yet the minister makes this suggestion. Because, during the war when there was a shortage of men and when there was surge of cargoes which had to be taken across the deep that our fighting forces might be kept effective, hazards had to be taken and life and liberty were in the balance-because these things were done then, the minister suggests that today we should depart from that age-old rule of stability of the law.
We come to section 40, concerning which there is no reason other than the convenience and the desire of a small departmental group to be absolute in their mastery of situations. What right has any man in any department to determine, without notice, how a ship shall be loaded or unloaded? What right has he to say how a passenger ship shall be equipped with lifesaving devices and others?
We talk here about our origin and about the majesty of the law. Not infrequently speakers are inclined to recall how a British sovereign summoned his judges together. If my memory serves me well, it was James I, in 1608-the very year in which Champlain came to the rock of Quebec-who did that. The judges of the court of king's bench of England were summoned one Sunday morning to ascertain if they would do the bidding of the king. They all, with the exception of one rather short, thick-necked, florid individual, bowed their heads and said they would. But one, Coke, who has achieved immortality, said it was not competent for anyone, even the king, to interfere with the courts. He stated a principle which has been accepted wherever institutions such as ours prevail, that is that all men are subject to the law at all times, namely, that

it is not competent to anyone at any time to change or to interfere with the law.
Yet by this bill the house is saying that fifty pages of a statute, upon which thousands of people depend for their safety may be stripped from the statutes; and the penalties which have heretofore attached to those who disregard these humanitarian provisions will cease to be effective.
We talk here frequently about communism and about the encroachments of communism upon our institutions. I suggest that we would do well to turn our eyes inward and look at the depredations going on in this very House of Commons where greater encroachments are being made upon the liberty of the subject and upon the stability of institutions built up through years of civilization than could ever be readily achieved by the activities of any foe from outside. We appear to have forgotten entirely what it cost to make of the law something durable, to make of the law something that applies to all men, something that could not be set aside, something that everybody was bound to respect, the integrity of which, both in its application and in its making, were beyond challenge.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Hazen):
That sections 11 and 40 of this bill be deleted.

I fail to see why the hon. member should be exercised at this stage about these particular sections. I fail to understand why he has selected these two rather than many others- several others, at least-of a similar nature which were brought in last session. I can think of an amendment to the Railway Act which I brought before the house, which had to do with an order in council arising out of the war emergency and which the house saw fit to approve. I can think of one or two like amendments brought in by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), which used practically the same wording as the orders in council passed during the war years.
Why my hon. friend should, because of a high legal principle, select these two sections in the act, is beyond me; because if the

Canada Shipping Act
principle he advocates is a good one, then it was a good one in the other instances to which I have referred.
My hon. friend made light, as he had a perfect right to do, of my explanation of the fact that this section 133A can be found in the Merchant Shipping Act of the United Kingdom. Not only can the section be found in that act, but the exact wording is used, with the exception of the substitution of the expression "board of trade" for the word "minister". I do not know whether my hon. friend is aware of the fact that the board of trade has now become the ministry of transport in the United Kingdom. So that over there the ministry of transport has the same rights and the same privileges as the Minister of Transport in this instance, on the advice of the steamship inspection board, seeks from the house.
Then it is set out that anything done by the minister under this section will be laid on the table of the house. I do not wish to go over the arguments I have already given, but I would say to the hon. member that this matter is urgent. Not only is it urgent in all parts of Canada where the shipping act applies, but particularly in his own province. If his amendments were to carry, there are various groups in the province of Quebec that would be seriously affected.
It has been found that shipowners have experienced extreme difficulty in securing dry-dock facilities for annual steamship inspection, because of the greater number of ships we now have. If these two sections are not allowed to remain in the act, ships would have to be tied up, not for weeks but for months. There could not be annual inspections of hulls, machinery and equipment as required under the Canada Shipping Act. The steamship inspection board can extend that inspection from one year to two years, if it is of the opinion that hulls, machinery and equipment are in seaworthy condition and safe to sail.
There are all sorts of difficulties arising in the manning of ships in connection with certificated officers and engineers. In order to keep ships moving, it is essential that these two sections be allowed to stand as they are. I would refer to some examples which would affect the position in my hon. friend's province.
There have been repeated occasions during the winter months when the Lapointe and the McLean had to go to the assistance of people who were in difficult straits on the north shore. Had it not been for these two sections, the ships could not have gone and could not
have taken the fuel, provisions and mail that these people on the north shore of the province of Quebec were awaiting.
The Magdalen islands have found themselves in similar difficult conditions; but because of these two sections it has been possible to send assistance and relief to the people of those islands, by exempting from part VII of the act certain of the necessary requirements.
I turn now to the province of Ontario where, because of this particular section, especially 488A, the extension of the summer and intermediate seasons to October 31 and December 1 for tankers between Toledo and certain other ports provided for hundreds of thousands of gallons of fuel oil. We know what the position with reference to fuel oil was last winter and what it will probably be again in the coming season. Had it not been for the relaxation of these requirements, fuel oil would have had to come by other than water transportation.
I could point to a number of occasions when paper products were sent to Corner Brook. Had the requirements been put into effect, ships would not have been able to take paper products to that part of Newfoundland. Operations under this amendment would be principally as follows:
1.	Extension of certificates where lack of drydock accommodation prevents inspections being completed.
2.	Acceptance of equipment considered sufficient pending delivery of required equipment on order.
3.	Acceptance of surveys by competent persons considered equivalent to steamship inspections.
4.	Permits for ships for occasional voyages beyond the limits of the inspection certificates.
5.	Permits for ships, recently operating under certificates other than Canadian, to allow continuous service until validity of existing certificates ceases.
6.	Increases in loading capacity of certain ships to carry bulk cargoes, ore, grain, coal and oil, during summer season.
7.	Permits for uncertificated engineers, pending examination for certificates.
I suggest that there is every reason why these two sections should be allowed. I would point to the experience in the United Kingdom where similar sections exist and where, by virtue of the commonwealth agreements, they are bound to respect our regulations as we are bound to respect theirs.
I say, finally, that if this amendment were allowed it would create great hardship to those
Canada Shipping Act

operating under the act, and particularly ships of this country would be tied up and would not be able to move with the dispatch that they should.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising at the earliest possible time in the budget debate in order to call the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his colleagues in the cabinet to matters which are of great concern to the people of British Columbia in the hope that, before the budget is finally passed, it may be found possible by the federal government to take steps to alleviate the financial problems which confront my province; also, may I say, to dispel the rankling sense of injustice which is felt by my people of British Columbia as the result of being the highest taxed province in the Dominion of Canada.
Of course the house is familiar with the many natural and climatic advantages of British Columbia which are of themselves of tremendous value to our economy. There are many wonderful features which result in our having the highest per capita income in the dominion, but those same features are not wholly economic assets. Equable climate and high wages have been a lure that has drawn tens of thousands of people from the other

The Budget-Mr. J. L. Gibson
provinces to our Pacific slopes. Younger people have gone there in a search for high wages and steady employment, while older people go there to bask in the sun in their declining years.
This rapid increase in our number can, in the long-term view, be considered an economic asset to our province, bringing as it does an increase in capital values of real estate and business concerns; but it will be realized by hon. members that sudden strain has been thrown on our provincial and municipal governments in having to provide schools, hospitals, social and domestic services to this large number of people.
From 1945 until the present these costs have been met from the provincial surplus account which was built up during the war years, when public expenditures were deferred in the interests of Canada's war effort; and I might tell the house that this surplus account of approximately 842,000,000 has now been entirely invested, either in deferred maintenance of our public works or in capital construction costs, which have built additional schools, hospitals, roads and university accommodation. In passing, may I say to hon. members that the University of British Columbia has increased its enrolment from 3,500 before the war to approximately 9,000 at the present time. These figures in themselves will give some idea of the sudden increase in the magnitude of the problems which this transition period has brought to my province.
I know the Minister of Finance may harbour the thought that the provincial authorities might have been wiser to retain part of this surplus as an emergency fund to bolster the revenue account in the event of an emergency, which now in fact has arisen; but may I point out to him that British Columbia is still a great frontier, has always been a country where the terrain enforces large highway and railroad expenditures in order that services may be provided to our scattered pockets of population. Consequently, our bonded indebtedness is now as high as prudence would indicate was desirable; and I am sure, too, that, in view of his own policy of reducing indebtedness out of surplus, the Minister of Finance cannot quarrel with provincial authorities if they are guided by his own example and follow the same course.

I know, sir, that the Minister of Finance can say with truth that these provincial receipts
The Budget-Mr. J. L. Gibson

from the federal government are only part of the complete story. He will point to family allowance payments, freight subsidies, public works expenditures, defence expenditures and a host of other federal spending within the provinces; but the fact remains that many of the residents of the one rich province which entered into the dominion-provincial agreement now feel that it was a sorry day for British Columbia when it agreed to bind itself with the other less wealthy provinces in an agreement with the federal government.
I may be asked, why did British Columbia enter into this arrangement? It must be admitted that there was no coercion used; but there was some very attractive bait held out and it was hoped that such a gesture from one of the so-called three wealthy provinces would set an example of co-operation and good will to Quebec and Ontario that might persuade them to make their contribution to Canadian unity and a more abundant life for all Canadian citizens, regardless of the province in which they happened to reside. I am sure that it was this feeling of good will and desire for higher standards of social services which prompted British Columbia's acceptance of the terms mutually agreed upon, plus the guarantee of minimum annual payments which would act as a floor to our provincial revenues in the event of an economic recession. Economic security seems to be the great goal in Canadian life today; but perhaps there is a valuable lesson to be learned there, by provincial governments as well as by individuals, that static security can be something for which we have to pay too high a price.
From the figures of provincial tax collections and receipts from the federal government, it can readily be seen that my province is making the highest per capita contribution to the federal treasury and receiving the least percentage of return. We receive approximately fifteen per cent back, compared with the next greatest contributor, Manitoba, which receives a return of approximately 20 per cent, down to the lowest-I exclude Prince Edward Island because I realize that there are special considerations affecting it-which is Saskatchewan, which receives a return from the federal treasury of approximately forty-one per cent of what it pays in, plus equal emoluments from other fields of federal expenditures. The situation can be stated perhaps more graphically on the basis of population. British Columbia, with approximately the same population as Saskatchewan, and most certainly with fewer members of parliament than

Saskatchewan, contributes $124 million net to the federal treasury, while Saskatchewan contributes $19,500,000. I cannot refrain from admonishing my C.C.F. friends from Saskatchewan who sit opposite-sometimes I think they are in a happy economic fog-that they should be very careful before they make any attempts to try to eradicate private enterprise from British. Columbia.

speechtext:
I know the Minister of Finance will be quick to point out that certain actions by the federal government have caused to a degree British Columbia's high income; that our foreign loans have made possible the high levels of profit and employment in our basic industries, and, to a degree, I believe this point to be well taken. He will admit, I know, that exports from every other province have been benefited to a lesser or greater degree, as has British Columbia, by the same methods; but I would ask him carefully to study this vital point: most of our wealth in British Columbia is coming from our extractive industries; in other words, we are using up our capital assets at a time of high federal taxation, and we cannot retain enough of this wealth under our present deal to pay the cost of opening up our remaining frontiers to development, the building of vital roads and railway lines and other public works which will make our reserves of timber, coal, minerals and agricultural land accessible at an economic level of cost to enable us to compete on world markets, which we inevitably must do.
The majority of the members of this house come from the two great central provinces, and they would be less than human if they did not at times become impatient with us members from the maritimes, and the western provinces who come here to this national forum at Ottawa and speak of the handicaps under which we labour. We speak of freight rate inequalities and discriminations; we ask

The Budget-Mr. J. L. Gibson
for lower tariffs on manufactured goods; we ask for co-operation from these two provincial governments that have chosen to remain outside the co-operative brotherhood of the dominion-provincial agreements, and they are perhaps tempted to think we are never satisfied.
To you from the two great manufacturing provinces, I would say: We do not begrudge you the necessary tariffs to enable your people to keep busy supplying us primary producers with the manufactured goods we require; only this, do not forget that our products must be sold in the competitive markets of the world; our pulp and paper, our lumber, our wheat, fish and apples, these you do not consume in adequate quantities to keep our economies solvent; you must co-operate with us economically if we are to continue to protect you behind tariff walls. There is no need for me to point out to you that in British Columbia, as in the maritimes and indeed in all the provinces which are at present cooperating with the dominion government, our natural and cheapest sources of supply for all manufactured goods is in the United States, and indeed that, too, is the natural market for most of the products which we produce.
Under the present financial arrangements with the federal government, all would be well, Mr. Speaker, if the people of British Columbia were paying the same rates of tax as the less wealthy provinces; but in order to care for our increase in expenditures, due, as I pointed out earlier, to the great increase in population, it has been necessary to place an additional tax burden on the British Columbia residents, namely a three per cent retail sales tax. As hon. members will realize, such a tax is extremely repugnant to any taxpayer anywhere; but especially is it so in British Columbia where, as I have pointed out, our per capita tax is the highest in the dominion. Another unfortunate feature of such a sales tax is that it inevitably increases our cost of production and, to that extent, impairs our competitive position in the export markets of the world upon which we must, in a large measure, depend for our livelihood.
I know the Minister of Finance will reply that perhaps the British Columbia government has gone ahead too rapidly in the field of social security measures. In reply to this, and by way of explanation, I will quote from the speech of Premier Byron Johnson, given in the British Columbia legislature on March 5 of this year. Mr. Johnson said:
At the time the Green Book proposals were presented to us, it was estimated by the dominion government that we would have a total of 16,670 old age pensioners on our lists by 1948. I find, however, that in October of
last year there were 17,768 persons in receipt of old age pensions and that now, the beginning of 1948, there are on our rolls 21,305 recipients. This figure is expected to rise to nearly 25,000 before the end of the year.
Or, as you will note, Mr. Speaker, fifty per cent over the estimate presented to them at the time the Green Book was brought out by the federal authorities. I continue with Mr. Johnson's remarks:
Since, due to climatic conditions, the bulk of internal emigration is toward the Pacific coast, British Columbia is placed in the position of making financial concessions through a tax agreement to what has been termed "less fortunate provinces," while at the same time being compelled to assume a very great share of the social service load of other provinces because of the emigration of their people to the coast... In short, 20 per cent of the new old age pension cases assumed during the last five months of 1947 were not really British Columbia cases in the true sense.
There has been a similar rapid rise in the number of persons receiving social allowances; that is, persons who are classified as unemployables. During the years from 1943 to 1945, inclusive, the increase was approximately 1,000 cases a year; but in 1946-47 the case-load rose by 2,000, and during the present fiscal year it is expected to rise by nearly 2,000 more . . .
In short, the cost of these three pensions alone has risen from $4,100,000 in 1945-46 to an estimated $8,900,000 in 1948-49, or by more than 100 per cent.
The inequality that exists between provinces with respect to social services can best he illustrated when it is pointed out that, despite British Columbia's rise in population, the per capita cost of these services has risen from $1.60 in 1944-45 to $2.07 in 1946-47. This is in contrast to Saskatchewan, where the per capita cost has risen merely from 56 cents to 76 cents.
I think they must all drift out to British Columbia when they reach the age where they qualify for social allowances. I continue:
Finally, in reviewing all social services, including both health and welfare, it was found that costs had risen from $9,300,000 in 1945-46 to an estimated $19,346,000 for 1948-49, or an increase of approximately $10,000,000 or more than 100 per cent.
I do not think that anyone would suggest that curtailment of expenditures should take place in our social services. It seemed to me, therefore, that if the dominion government, by virtue of our withdrawal from the income, corporation, and succession duty tax fields could collect $139,-
958,000	from this province during the fiscal year ended March 31st, 1947, and pay back to the province approximately $23,000,000, or only i6 per cent of what they collected, it was reasonable to expect that the social security proposals of the Green Book should be implemented, if only partially.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the views of the Liberal Premier of British Columbia. I am sure that the Minister of Finance, if he were in his seat at the moment, and the parliamentary assistant to the minister who comes
The Budget-Mr. J. L. Gibson

from British Columbia, would both say that our premier is a man of unimpeachable integrity and sound business judgment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will be the last to do anything.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the hon. member is getting a bit worked up. There is no point in merely urging complaints without offering some solution; and I shall try to keep my suggestions for budget revisions to orthodox practices, which I am sure are the only kind that our present Minister of Finance will accept, in any event. Let us first examine the 1947-48 surplus as reported by the Minister of Finance last Tuesday. He said it amounted to $650 million which, as he said, was a figure to gladden the heart of any minister of finance. In my view that was a very modest statement.
I am sure that Canadians generally will take encouragement from the fact that our heavy tax payments were not entirely dissipated by federal expenditure, but let me express my own personal views in regard to this surplus.
First of all, it was approximately $500 million more than was estimated by himself in conjunction with his financial advisers and experts, and this huge surplus does not, in my opinion, prove that they were bad guessers. It resulted almost entirely from the processes of inflation and merely reflects the fallacious over-confidence of the government that they would be able to control inflation in Canada.
Their inability to control inflation in Canada to the degree which they expected resulted in high costs, higher wages, higher provincial expenditures and provincial deficits, but in the case of the federal government the net result was a $500 million increase in the expected surplus.
This surplus, by no stretch of anyone's imagination or conscience, can be assumed to be solely the property of the dominion government; surely the provincial governments should have a little consideration shown them. I admit that when we retire federal debt w'e are repaying debts which every citizen in Canada owes; but surely when the senior government has a surplus and there is personal and municipal and provincial hardship because of conditions which created that surplus, then I submit that the guilty conscience of the finance minister should have spurred him to display "a humble and contrite heart" in consulting the provinces as to how a part of this huge and unexpected surplus could be used to mitigate the burden of more junior taxing authorities.
Despite what I have said regarding the apparent inequalities of British Columbia's

tax payments, I appreciate the fact that the minister must treat all provinces, rich and poor, on the same basis, and I would not ask him to do otherwise.
This is what I suggest that he do immediately :
1.	Set up a federal highway commission which would designate the highways to be considered as links in the trans-Canada highway system.
2.	Pay in cash to the provinces twenty-five per cent of the capital and maintenance cost which they have spent on these highways during the past ten years.
3.	Offer to contribute twenty-five per cent to the capital and maintenance costs of any such designated new highways if undertaken at any time, with the further proviso that such commission have authority to contribute up to 50 per cent of the capital costs of such federal highway construction, if undertaken at the instance of the federal government when surplus labour and material are available.
4.	Make money available to provincial governments at cost of 2J per cent for construction costs of schools and hospitals, interest only to be deducted from the provincial grants for a transitional period of ten years, after that time amortization to start over a period of the next forty years.
5.	An agreement with the provinces to be entered into which will guarantee a minimum return of twenty per cent of corporate and personal income tax collections in that province.
Mr. Speaker, the creation of such a federal or trans-Canada highway board is a step which I am sure would meet with the approval of every member of this house, as may be confirmed by reference to speeches made by members on all sides during the past years. The arguments are too numerous and too well known for me to repeat them at this time, but I know that every Canadian looks forward to the day when there will be a highway across Canada, from sea to sea, from Yarmouth in Nova Scotia to Tofino on the west coast of Vancouver island.
I advance these proposals to the federal government in the hope that they will give them serious study and consideration. Some means must be found to assist and guide our junior governments. It is idle to talk of 1941 provincial tax collections as a valid basis for discussion ; since that date, great changes have taken place in productivity, population, and capital investment as between the various provinces and, moreover, we no longer are speaking of the same dollar. It used to mean 100 cents; its purchasing power in labour and materials is now only sixty cents.

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
In closing. Mr. Speaker, may I express the hope that this government will immediately re-examine the position of the provinces; and I am confident that, with tolerance, sympathy and understanding on both sides, a fair and reasonable compromise can be arrived at.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to compliment the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) on the speech he has just delivered. It was one of the best I have heard him give. I hope, of course, he will vote in the manner he spoke. If he does, I am sure he will vote against the budget which is before us today.
Despite what most members of the house probably think about the budget before us today, I am sure all will agree that last Tuesday evening, the Minister of Finance (Mr, Abbott) delivered a comprehensive and lucid statement. It is almost certain, I think, that this budget will reach a new high as an unpopular measure, and in view of that fact the minister is to be complimented on having had the personal courage to proceed with it as he did.
Having prefaced my remarks with that comment, I must say that in my opinion this budget is unnecessarily harsh. Seldom in recent years have the Canadian people waited for a budget with such eagerness, but I am sure that never in recent years have they been disappointed so thoroughly and completely.
In a nutshell, what does this budget report and what does it propose? It reports, in the first place, a surplus which is larger than all the surpluses which we have had, put together, since confederation. It reports, in the second place, that the recent year was as prosperous economically as we have ever had. Yet, despite these facts, the minister has the audacity to come to parliament, and suggest that next year Canadian taxpayers shall be given no relief of any consequence.
This group cannot concur with that recommendation. We believe that the rising cost of living has made it imperative that taxpayers, particularly those in the lower categories, shall be given tax relief at this time. If parliament refuses to grant this concession within the next few days, I think unnecessary hardships are bound to result.
I find the figures on the revenue side of the budget most revealing. Hon. members who heard the budget speech last year will remember that the minister said, as reported at page 2610 of Hansard:
Behind us are the huge and difficult budgets of the war years.
"Behind us"; and yet during the recent fiscal year the minister collected in taxes from the Canadian people $2,630 million. During the last year of the war the government's tax revenues were only $2,374 million. In other words, in the past year Canadians were taxed more heavily by $256 million than in the last year of the war. I find it hard it reconcile that fact with the promise the minister gave last year that the huge budgets of the war years were behind us. The burden of taxation can be realized when we compare it with our taxes in 1938, the last year of peace. In that year our taxes were $516 million, or only one-fifth of their present level.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about income?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am talking about taxes. During the war years Canadians willingly paid high taxes and made many sacrifices. But the war has been over three years. I do not think it was ever contemplated that huge governmental taxes should roll forward indefinitely into the years of peace. Every member of parliament should realize that the people of Canada are aroused over the fact that parliament has not seen fit to give them some decrease in taxation at this time.
The expenditure side of the ledger is also disconcerting when you look at the budget. The minister reports little progress in reducing the cost of government. Last year the total expenditure amounted to $2,124 million, and in his budget speech the minister said, as reported at page 4057 of Hansard:
We have striven to bring expenditures down and to keep them down.
Yet in the next breath he forecast, for the coming year, general expenditures amounting to $51,000,000 more than last year. Furthermore, he forecast that there would be additional expenditures to be announced later in the year. At a time when approximately twenty per cent of the national income is going into federal taxation, many Canadians are wondering whether the government is doing all that is possible to curtail its ordinary expenditures.
The minister informed the house that this year we shall have a surplus of $727 million. While we are on these surpluses, it is interesting to remember that last session the minister forecast a surplus of only $190 million. In other words, in his calculations he apparently made an error of $537 million. If he has made the same error this year, we shall have a surplus of over one billion dollars in the coming fiscal period.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He listened to your gloomy
forecasts of last year.
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I must say that I agree with the principle of budgeting for a surplus in times of prosperity, with certain qualifications. On the other hand I want to say that this surplus has not been achieved by economies; rather it has been achieved, in large part, by imposing vicious indirect sales and excise taxes; by refusing the taxpayer any relief from excessive personal income tax; by failing to carry out an adequate system of social services; and by refusing to go ahead with such projects as were mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, namely a trans-Canada highway, irrigation works in the west and things like that. I am sure this budget will go down in history as a monument to government neglect. I think the minister should not be too proud of the surplus he is showing us today.
However, after he achieved the surplus, most Canadians thought they would be given some tax relief, and I think justifiably so. Yet the tax relief which the minister is proposing for 1&18-49 is almost negligible. Suppose we look at the tax relief for a moment. First of all, the minister announced he is going to remove the sales tax on certain foodstuffs. That is a trifling concession, although it is welcome.

Not at all, but probably British Columbia has imposed the tax. I suggest that this tax on amusements will not be passed on to the consumer in most cases, so that it means very little to him.
The minister announced cuts in the British tariff on rayons and and cotton piece goods. Let me say that this concession is most welcome. But once again, without price ceilings, I do not think these concessions will reach the consumer. I am much afraid they will be absorbed by the dealers in those commodities, whether they be wholesalers, retailers or agents.
The minister announced that he was going to reduce the succession duty tax. Henceforth, when anyone dies, his estate will not be taxed if it is not one of $50,000 or over. Formerly it was taxed if it was $5,000 or over. It seems strange to me that a man must die in order to get tax relief from the Liberal government, but apparently that is the case.
The minister announced a few other trifling concessions. He said he was taking the tax off vinegar, silver ware and alarm clocks. The hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight) received a letter about this alarm clock concession, and I should like to read a quotation from it, which is as follows:
Someone should send Mr. Abbott an alarm clock at the reduced rate in order to wake him up to the needs of the people.
That sums up the matter quite well. In other words, I suggest that the tax concessions the minister has made in this budget are trifling. They do not mean much to the average taxpayer. With regard to personal income tax, the only concession the minister made was to people sixty-five years of age and over; he gave them an increased exemption of $500. But the great majority of taxpayer's were given absolutely no relief whatever. Indeed, instead of relief, today they are forced to pay stiffer penalties if they should happen to be late in filing their income tax forms. With the ever increasing cost of living, the income tax has almost reached the point of confiscation. The real income of many citizens has been cut so much by inflation that some families cannot afford to buy milk, cannot afford to buy-

The government's treatment of the small wage earner is to be deplored all the more when we remember that, at the first of the year, they took off the excess profits tax, and they took it off at a time when corporation profits were higher, probably, than they have ever been in our history.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the scarcity of their numbers in the chamber, I am afraid I am going to have a little trouble in convincing many Liberals tonight. However, when the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the failure of the government to give tax relief in this budget to the people of Canada, at a time when the government has shown an overwhelming surplus of $727 million.
I had stated that in my opinion this budget is unnecessarily harsh. It has given little or no tax relief to Canadians at a time when the cost of living has rendered such relief imperative. I suggested, moreover, that in refusing this relief the government is riding roughshod over the wishes of about ninety-nine per cent of the adult population.
I suggest now that for a few moments we should look at the reasons the minister gave in his budget speech for refusing tax relief.
His first reason was the need to pay off some of the national debt. To a degree I can go along with that policy. In times of prosperity it is only sensible that some of the debt we accumulated during war years should be paid off. But I believe there is a point of balance between desirable debt reduction and the public's ability to pay it. The minister
does not seem to have found that balance. It is one thing to skim off surplus excess earnings and quite another thing to impoverish large parts of the population in the process of skimming. I suggest that the minister could have given reasonable tax relief, at least in the lower brackets, without seriously impairing his debt reduction program.
The second reason the minister gave for refusing tax relief had to do with defence. I quote from page 4063 of Hansard where he says:
We face today very great uncertainties in international affairs ... A substantial surplus will help to keep our powder dry.
The minister implied that Canada has certain military responsibilities which she must look after, in a democratic world. On the surface that reason looks fairly plausible. But I find, as I read the page a little farther down, that the minister this year is budgeting $20,000,000 less for defence expenditures than he did last year. I find it hard to understand this fact, if the peril to Canada is as alarming as he says it is. It strikes me that he is not suiting his actions to his words.
The minister stated, in the third place, that high taxes were necessary to combat inflation. Once again I quote from his speech, as it appears in Hansard:
We should deliberately budget, as a matter of policy, for substantial surpluses in times like these. Only that way can we hold inflationary forces in check.
I ask the house to note that. I think the minister knows that statement is not correct. The suggestion that high taxation is the most effective way of controlling inflation is worn out. High taxation in the past few years has not prevented prices from going up; nor will high taxes in the future prevent inflation from continuing. It contributes to the inflationary spiral, instead of taking away from it and stopping it.
Surely the minister would not suggest to the house that a policy of giving a little tax relief to small wage earners might start an orgy of buying. The government's taxation policy, instead of stopping inflation, is adding to it. Such taxes as the sales tax and the excise tax contribute directly to the high cost of living. If the government is really sincere in its desire to fight inflation at this time I suggest that it set an example by removing some of these indirect taxes.
Then it seems to me that the minister is being inconsistent when, on the one hand, he makes the claim that taxes cannot be reduced because it would place extra purchasing power in the hands of the taxpayers, thereby raising the cost of living, but on the other hand-
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher

just a little later in his budget-tells us he is going to give an extra year's compulsory savings back to Canadians who paid them originally. That will release about $80,000,000 extra purchasing power the minister did not have to release.
The minister cannot have it both ways. If it is possible to risk redistributing $80,000,000 in that manner, then surely there could have been a reduction in taxes.
I suggest to the house, that inflation could have been controlled much more effectively and much more equitably by price control, than it has been by high taxation. At page 4057 of Hansard, the minister made this statement:
It would have been more comfortable had we been able to return to a free price system under general conditions of stability, balanced production and abundant imports.
Of course it would. That is precisely what this party has been trying to point out for two years, both in parliament and out of parliament. Then the minister went on to say that he could not keep controls because, "fate did not afford us that opportunity."
Well, that statement is hardly correct. It was not fate which took off controls prematurely; it was the Liberal party. Today we are seeing the folly of that action. Canadian citizens are paying heavily for the error in judgment which the Liberal party made.
The other day the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) described the prices committee as a fiasco. From the view point of the Progressive Conservative party, perhaps it is a fiasco. Certainly I do not think their members have been anxious to make it a success. Certainly the findings of the prices committee-

I shall withdraw it; I meant to say it did not seem that way to me. Certainly the findings of the committee have been harmful to the political philosophy in which the Progressive Conservative party believes. Perhaps in that regard it has been a fiasco.

When the prices committee was originally set up, the C.C.F. group argued that this was not the way to solve Canada's inflation problem. We are still of the same opinion. We believe that only the reimposition of price controls can cope with the inflation problem; and I think that contention has been borne out by the facts.
Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott.)1 told us in debate that prices would stabilize around an index of 146. The index has climbed steadily, until today it is 151, and it is still going up.
However, once the prices committee was set up, members of this group have tried to make it useful. Our members attended regularly. Personally I believe the committee has done some valuable work. I believe by this time it has discovered, beyond any reasonable doubt, the main reason for the ever-rising cost of living. Because of the devastation of the war, and because of the abnormal conditions arising from the war, the demand for most goods has been far in excess of the supply. Under these circumstances regular competition is not functioning to keep prices down.
In the committee, one witness after another has freely admitted taking advantage of shortages to make the largest possible profits. That is natural under the present economic set-up. In the committee I asked one witness after another to suggest some voluntary way in which we could bring prices down. Not one witness has, to my knowledge, given us any idea of how this could be done voluntarily.

speechtext: On a point of order, I do not think the hon. member is allowed to discuss the evidence given before a committee.
