It has been agreed that hon. members may discuss the general situation with respect to prices, but they should not discuss what is going on in the committee.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Before you insist upon that ruling, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might make several comments?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just stick to the rules of
the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the first place, I would state that the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario mentioned prices the other day. In the second place, the Minister of Finance has stated that high taxation is the way to

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
control inflation. My argument is that price controls would be a more effective way. In the third place, when the prices committee was set up, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, if I understood him correctly, that debate in the house on the subject would not be precluded.
I have not very much more to say about the matter, but I should like to put my opinion on record. I believe it is a better way of controlling inflation than the budget of the Minister of Finance. If that is satisfactory,
I shall proceed; if I am out of order, I shall stop.
When the committee was set up, the Prime Minister suggested that the glare of unfavourable publicity would probably bring down prices. I think the proceedings have shown that that hope is futile. The committee has found why prices are up and, if the government will give the committee teeth, I think we can get prices down.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is all this in order?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I ask the hon. gentleman again not to discuss what has gone on in the prices committee.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you. I will not mention the discussions again. The Minister of Finance has told us repeatedly that our economy is tied up with the economy of the United States. During the last month costs and prices in that country have gone up to a higher level than ever before. The federal reserve board is predicting that inflationary pressure in the United States will be greater in the last six months of this year than it was in the first six months. That is caused by the huge European recovery program together with a tremendous $14,000 million expenditure for military affairs which the United States are making.
So serious has the situation become in the United States, that the President's economic advisory committee recently recommended price controls, as the only effective way to stop run-away inflation in that country. Here in Canada the situation is similar, and it seems to me the government is being very stubborn when it refuses to recognize that fact. No one likes controls. When the supply of merchandise and produce can catch up with the demand, by all means get rid of controls; but until that time let us be sensible. Let the government admit they erred; let them, even at this late moment, have the courage .to correct their error. Let us stop this steady rise in the cost of living.
The fourth reason the minister gave for keeping taxation high was to conserve United States dollars, and that suggestion struck me
5849-274J
as the weakest argument of all. Surely the export-import controls which parliament set up a few months ago should be able to do this effectively. On page 4063 of Hansard the minister states:
We must build up an export surplus-we must try to export more or import less, or both.
Despite that statement, despite the fact that the minister says he needs United States dollars very badly, in his budget he overlooks the' huge amount of United States dollars which are available, if the embargo on Canadian cattle and other agricultural products entering the United States is lifted. This would be a lucrative source of United States exchange, some people estimating it at $100,000,000. If we need United States dollars so badly, why is the-minister neglecting that source? The minister is always talking about a free economy. It seems strange to me that all controls have been taken off except those which affect the farmer.
For these reasons this group cannot agree with the minister in his contention that the taxpayer should not be given any relief at this time. Along with the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario, I must say I am wondering whether tax relief is being held over until next year for partly political reasons. Certainly, if substantial tax reductions were given a year from now they could be translated more effectively into political advantage. I suggest that this budget is not a human budget; I think it could be better described as a Tory budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Next year's budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is only one other matter I should like to deal with. I am sorry the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario is not in his seat at the moment. On page 4249 of Hansard the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario implied that democratic socialism-in Canada the C.C.F. party-is similar to nazism, fascism and communism. The hon. member is a man whom I personally admire very much, and I regret that he should have made a suggestion of that kind, because I realize he knows it is not correct. As every hon. member in this house knows, the C.C.F. party has refused time and again to co-operate in any way with communism or with any other ism.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or with anybody else.

I have inquired into the communist party and studied Earl Marx. Knowing their philosophy, I feel it is false and I believe it is wrong from the economic, moral and sociological standpoints.

Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Mr. Speaker, the house is engaged in the discussion of a travesty of a budget. The esteemed leader of the Progressive Conservative party has properly described it as the worst budget since confederation, and we of the Progressive Conservative party are one in denouncing this budget as a shockingly harsh imposition on the Canadian people.
A year ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) boasted of his budget surplus, but the budget surplus he reported to the house last Tuesday evening is apparently proving something of an embarrassment to him. Whence did this surplus come? In the first place, it is the product of very bad budgeting. It represents an all-time high in inaccurate budgeting. What was forecast a year ago as a budget surplus of $190 million, now appears as a surplus of $670 million, or a cash surplus of $1,181 million. Yes, one way it is three and a half times what was forecast, and the other way it is six times as much as was forecast. It is impossible, therefore, for any member of this house to approach the present budget and its forecasts with any measure of confidence in the size of budget surplus that has been forecast by the Minister of Finance.

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
Where did this budget surplus come from? What is the source of it? The source is the very same source from which the government always obtains its money. It has no magic source of money. The source from which the government gets its money is the pockets of the people, and in this case, what we find is that a surplus has been created because the government dipped far more deeply into the pockets of the people than there was any need for their doing. And now the Minister of Finance says: I am going to budget for a further surplus, a surplus of $489 million. If his forecast is no more accurate than that of a year ago we may expect a year hence that he will be announcing a budget surplus anywhere from one and a half to two billion dollars, if the same ratio of inaccuracy is maintained.
The taxpayer deserves a break, not the beating that this government is giving to him. The reductions are so trifling as to be insignificant in relation to the size of the tax load that is being maintained on the back of the taxpayer, and they are trifling in relation to the needs of the taxpayer. Never has there been a stronger case than today for tax reductions; but the Minister of Finance, apart from insignificant little reductions, haB slammed shut the door in the face of the taxpayer who has asked and rightly expected some substantial reduction in the load of taxation.
The authors of this budget have shown they do not know anything about the problems of those who are called upon to pay these shockingly heavy imposts. They just do not know, for they could not possibly justify these tax proposals if they did. It will, I am sure, shock every member of this house to find the Minister of Finance saying, as he did on May 18, at page 4057 of Hansard:
There will never be a better time to reduce the burden of our national debt. We can do it now without hardship.
I say, Mr. Speaker, he cannot do it on this scale without hardship. He has been pursuing this policy in recent years, not without hardship, but at the expense of hardship on the Canadian people. There is hardship now on the part of hundreds of thousands of Canadians in trying to make both ends meet; but apparently the Minister of Finance and the members of the government are so far removed from the experience of the rank and file of the Canadian peple in meeting their family budgetary problems, that they just do not know anything about the problems these families are experiencing in trying to make both ends meet.
This weight of taxation, not suddenly imposed, but continued year after year after year, from war into peace, and now after three years of peace carried into the fourth year of peace, represents confiscation. It can no longer be called taxation; it is now confiscation. In the case of a great many Canadians it represents today a capital levy, because there are many families in Canada living on a small income who simply cannot meet the high cost of living and the burden of taxation without having to borrow on their insurance policies and try to get by in that way. These continued imposts represent a capital levy in the case of these people. But the government apparently does not know anything about the plight of the people who are living today on a small income. It does not seem to realize what the vaulting cost of living means to these people, the wage earners and those who are living on a low, fixed salary.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, this budget is likely to defeat one of the purposes which the minister professed in introducing it. It is likely to lead to more labour unrest. It cannot fail to evoke, on the part of many sections of labour, demands for increased wages in order that they may meet this double load of the high cost of living and high taxation, and to the extent that it may give rise to labour unrest it will set back production and give a further fillip to inflation.
There is the further factor to which this government is both deaf and blind. It is the fact that the people want tax reductions. Who is supreme in this country, Mr. Speaker? Is it the government, this group of nineteen men, or is it the people of Canada, the people who are paying the shot? Those of us who are perhaps a little old-fashioned in our views thought the people wrere supposed to be supreme; and one might have hoped, if that were true, that the views of the people in demanding relief from this load of taxation might have been heard and that the government might have given some heed to this clamour for relief from the load of taxation. But apparently it is not to be so with this government. This is a different kind of government. With this government in office, it seems that the people are not supreme. The government fancies itself supreme and, no matter what the people may think, no matter what they may rightly and justly expect and demand, this government is nevertheless saying to them: No, you shall have no reductions.
I happened to be in Washington during the Easter recess, on the day on which congress overrode the President's veto of its tax reduction bill. That was a victory of the people. That was a victory of public opinion over the
_________The Budget-Mr. Fleming

executive branch of government, and I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is high time we in this country had a victory of public opinion over the dictates of the executive branch of government here. Our system of government is not like that which obtains in the United States. Apparently the only way that the people of Canada can have an opportunity of asserting public opinion, when this government is too deaf to hear or too blind to read the signs of the times, is by recourse to the ballot; therefore this party has in its amendment challenged this government to carry this issue to the people in a general election. This is a government that has been far too long in office now for the good of Canada.

speechtext: What have you to offer in its place?

speechtext:
A government that will be just 100 per cent improvement over the ramshackle, dying government at present on the treasury benches will take its place.
This budget also raises searching questions as to the fundamental and underlying purpose of taxes. The theory, recognized from the beginning of responsible government until the present time, until the era of this government, has been that taxes were an impost upon the people to meet the legitimate expenses of government. But, apparently we have to recast our thinking entirely in the light of this budget, because it bears no relationship whatsoever to the needs of meeting legitimate expenses of government. This house will not cavil about meeting those expenses, but it will cavil about being asked to levy upon the Canadian people such an additional amount as bears no relationship whatever to the legitimate expenses of government or to the needs of retirement of the national debt in due time.
Yes, back of , this budget is a fetish, which apparently has seized hold of this government, that somehow it is its duty to prevent the people of Canada from using their own money. Whose money is it, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada are toiling to earn? The government thinks this money is its own and it has first call on it, and the poor wage earners may take what is left. The people of 'Canada, I affirm, do not need the paternalistic Intrusion of this government into their affairs to help them manage their own finances in their own family budgets. They do not need this government to step in to try to prevent them from using their own money, whether by way of satisfying their own obligations or saving or spending their money.
The Minister of Finance has assumed, all the way through his budget speech, that the money would be used entirely by the people of 
Canada, whatever would be saved to them in reduction of taxes, by running out and spending it at once. He does not know the Canadian people, and neither does any member of the government who supports this budget on that basis. The Canadian people know best what to do with their own affairs and what to do with their own earnings, and if there is any undue disposition on the part of any to spend today it is probably due in no small measure to the way this government has discouraged their saving money and being thrifty.
Yes, this budget has all the earmarks of paternalism; it has all the earmarks of robbery when one considers the proper sphere of taxation in meeting the legitimate expenditures of government.

Certainly I will withdraw the word, Mr. Speaker, if you say so. I have heard it used in the house before, but I will certainly withdraw it if you say so and I will substitute' for it, "the absolutely unjustified and unconstitutional imposition".
Indeed, it is the kind of budget that is the product of the brain trust. It is not taxation; it is not a budget to be measured in terms of taxation. It has no relationship to taxation needs. You can think of this, Mr. Speaker, only in terms of confiscation; and it springs out of a desire to foist upon Canada a scheme of managed economy. This budget is intended to be a weapon in foisting a managed economy upon Canada.
It is not new to find the government pursuing the path of managed economy. Here is a member of the government on the C.B.C. network last August 6 speaking on behalf of the Liberal party:
My guess is that any future government in Canada, whatever its political complexion, will resort to some type of economic planning.
These are the words of Senator Robertson, the government leader in the senate. In this budget, Mr. Speaker, you see some of the fruits of that mentality on the part of the

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
government, a mentality that believes in the managed economy. Here is an expression that the Minister of Finance has used, which I suggest has some significance. At page 4063 of Hansard, he is reported as saying:
This government and this parliament must accept a considerable measure of responsibility for influencing and, indeed, directing economic trends in so far as that can be done within the framework of our political and economic principles.
Further on, he refers to the government as:
Those charged with responsibility of directing the affairs of the nation as a whole.
No one will have any objection to the efficient management of the affairs of the Dominion of Canada within the proper sphere of government; but where we take issue, and complete issue, with this budget is that it intrudes into the affairs of the people; it intrudes into their private affairs, and seeks to set the government up in the management of these private affairs. I ask the minister to listen to his own words as recorded at page 4056 of Hansard:
Neither this government nor this parliament has either the political mandate or the constitutional power to maintain indefinitely in peacetime a strait-jacket of controls over prices, production and distribution. Our whole economy has been organized to operate on a price basis by private incentives and pi'ivate initiatives, not by centralized direction. I believe that the great majority of Canadians want it to work that way, want it to work by free and open competition and not by government direction on the one hand nor on the other hand by direction of the irresponsible power of monopolies, artels and other organized groups.
Theoe are good words, Mr. Speaker. I just wish that the minister would apply them to this bare-faced attempt to further the schemes of those who believe in the managed economy. This government has no mandate from the people of Canada to impose a system of managed economy upon this country.
It is just impossible to conceive that any government would bring in so bad and so harsh a budget unless it had some card up its sleeve; and therefore we are left to think that the card is to be played in 1949 with some reductions then, on which the government will seek to make a grandstand show on the eve of a general election. Well, they insult the intelligence and the memory of the people of Canada if they think they are going to live down the recollection of this woeful budget so soon. Yes, retribution will await this government whenever it dares to submit itself to the Canadian people.
This budget is an irresponsible budget. It has been born in the same kind of mind as conceived, first, those dictatorial import
restrictions last fall, and, second, taxation by radio, that gross invasion of the constitutional privileges of Canadians. It is the same mentality at work. There has been no reform since November 17, 1947. This country and this government are in the grip of those who believe in the managed economy. I for one do not believe in the managed economy. One reason I do not believe in it is that there is not enough intelligence in any man's mind, or in the mind of any small group of men to manage the whole of the Canadian economy. In the second place, Mr. Speaker, it is far too dangerous to be risked, because any mistake made, where you have a system of managed economy, is on so vast a scale that the results are bound to be catastrophic. We are not without experience in Canada of the colossal scale on which the effects of the blunders of the managed economy theorists are likely to make themselves felt. We have had a sample of it in this country since the great blunder in the middle of 1946 and the constant flight of United States dollars from Canada ever since, a flight and a policy which almost brought this country to economic ruin in 1947.
Let me examine ever so briefly some of the reasons put forward by the Minister of Finance. He has trotted out the bogey of inflation and has suggested that this budget is likely in some way to assist in deterring the inflationary processes now at work. We have inflation now. This kind of taxation has not restrained the processes of inflation. The minister has the idea, and I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, it is a fundamental fallacy in his whole approach to the problem, that if he helps to boost prices higher by adding more taxes he will help to restrain the inflationary process.
The suggestion is so utterly foolish on the face of it that it amazes one that it should be put forward by a minister in this house. The minister had a great opportunity, the opportunity of a lifetime, to reduce taxation and make a substantial contribution to the reduction in the cost of living. Yes, he could have done much to mitigate the present rigours of inflation which are bearing so heavily upon persons of small means and small fixed incomes in Canada. If the removal of the sales tax on prepared foods was sound, then, Mr. Speaker, why would it not be sound to extend that removal to a great many other commodities which enter into the cost of living of the Canadian family?
The minister has sought to continue, yes, and has justified the continued imposition of these hidden consumer taxes which bear
The Budget-Mr. Fleming

relatively so much more heavily on the man of small means, because they are consumer taxes. These taxes levied at the source, on the manufacturer, go on pyramiding as they pass from one hand to another, until the sales tax, starting at eight per cent in the hands of the manufacturer, is invariably about fifteen per cent when the consumer pays the price of the goods over the counter. In addition to that, you have all the excise taxes that go on heaping burden upon burden on the ultimate consumer with every hand through which they travel.
What about economy? If only we could have some evidence on the part of the government that it believes in economy and is making an honest, frank effort to approach the problem with a view to effecting reasonable economies in the operation of government; not to do away with essential services, but to grapple with the problem of eliminating unnecessary expenditures of government! A government which has the belief that it is contributing to the restraint of the processes of inflation by boosting prices through the inclusion of high taxes in them, is certainly not the kind of government that has the ghost of a chance of doing anything to effect necessary economies in the cost of government.
By entertaining such a belief, the government has disabled itself before it even starts. There is no use in expecting economy from this government when it has started already with the idea that it is restraining inflation by heaping taxation on top of the high prices of commodities today.
_ We believe that within reasonable limits the idea of putting aside a surplus when times are good, and reducing the debt when times are good, is sound, but not when you find it on the scale practised here. What would the individual do? An individual who has some idea of his responsibility puts aside some money for the rainy day. But have we any assurance that this government, simply because it is soaking the taxpayer today far beyond its own needs, will give any benefit to the taxpayer when times are not so good? Should a recession come, is there any assurance that there will be a reduction in taxation?
There is no such assurance. As a matter of fact, when that time comes we may find pressures at work in the other direction. If it is the kind of government that we have today-which heaven forbid!-the government would say: Well, we have increased expenditures now to meet additional costs; therefore we must keep up the taxes to meet the cost. And the government will just go on, in those 
days as it is doing now, by its taxation policies, penalizing thrift and hard work.
There is no guarantee here that the sacrifices made today will be passed on should a recession in business conditions come. And it is not as though this burden of taxation were newly laid upon us. The Canadian people have been carrying it for years, and carrying it in the hope that sometime this burden would be lifted and they would see the daylight. Last year the government paid off five per cent of the net national debt, and it is budgeting now to pay an additional four per cent of that debt. It is going much too fast in that direction.
This managed economy idea is of the essence of socialism. The socialists believe in the managed economy. They believe that government, simply because it is government, can manage the affairs of the people, can manage the economy of the country, including the affairs of families throughout Canada, the budgets of Canadian homes, better than the Canadian people can manage these things themselves.
You find that same thought inherent in the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), because, after dealing with the question of increasing exemptions in income tax and reducing the burden of the sales tax, he adds this in his amendment:
And further, the government has failed to establish a public investment board to assure the channelling of capital investment into socially desirable projects as a means of maintaining full employment, increasing production and raising the standard of living of the Canadian people.
Everyone in this house, I think, believes in full employment, increasing production and raising the standard of living, but I hope we do not believe in the method that is proposed here by usurping in favour of the government the right to say how money shall be invested in Canada. What is the capacity of government for directing investment of money?
This is a further example of the centralization of power that is inherent in the socialist creed in this country; and it is for reasons of that kind that, no matter how members of the C.C.F. may dislike communist support, the communists can see themselves so closely identified with the C.C.F. I have not said that the C.C.F. see themselves identified with the communists. Many members of the C.C.F. in this house have disavowed communist support; but the fact is that communist support is still forthcoming, and in the present election in Ontario we have Tim Buck, No. 1 communist in Canada,

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
calling upon communists throughout Ontario to back the C.C.F. candidates in every riding where there is no communist candidate.

I do know that the sense of discipline in the communist party is strong, and Tim Buck has told communists throughout Ontario-he said so publicly; there is no secret about it-to vote for the C.C.F. candidates in every riding where there is no communist candidate, and there are only two ridings in the province where there are communist candidates. The matter does not stop there. You will remember the blatant offer that Tim Buck made of support to the C.C.F. throughout Canada when he advocated the election of a C.C.F. government. He calls for a C.C.F. victory:
If we elect a C.C.F. government in. Ottawa, it is quite obvious that the whole perspective for Canada will be changed. Certainly then our road ahead will be through the social democratic regime. . . After we have elected a C.C.F. government and we are faced with the question of how to work further to develop socialist consciousness in the majority of the working class, we can truly say that the party that did this is a Marxist party, the part of socialist Canada.
I was interested to hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatoher) in his speech tonight deal with the subject. It is not long ago that Mr. Laski, who was chairman of the executive of the labour party in Great Britain at the time of the last election, and who is regarded as one of the leading mouthpieces of that party there, had some things to say on the subject of the position of the socialist party in Great Britain. If the C.C.F. is such a democratic party, how do they account for the fact that Mr. Laski-and I am using his words-expressed doubt "whether in a period of transition the Labour government"-by that he meant, of course, the socialist government- "could risk overthrow of its measures as the result of a general election"? Does that sound like democracy, saying they are not going to risk a general election if it means that their socialist measures would be put in jeopardy? This same Mr. Laski is the author of a book entitled "Faith, Reason and Civilization". It is a neat little book. I wish to quote from pages 57 and 58 of it, in which Mr. Laski expresses his great admiration for the Russian system. These are his words:
The solemn truth remains that in the Soviet Union more men and women have had more opportunity of self-fulfilment than anywhere else in the world ... it is the only nation which . . . knows without doubt that its people
move to the control of their own destiny . . . If therefore it be accepted that our own time bears a profound resemblance to the era in which Christianity was born, it seems to me that we are entitled to conclude that the regeneration of values which the new faith effected, after no doubt a long and bitter struggle, is more likely to be secured in our own age by the central idea of the Russian revolution than by any alternative principle we are in a position to choose.
That is Mr. Laski in a book published in 1944, judt the year before the last general election in Great Britain. The C.C.F. say that socialism is necessarily democratic. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the communists are clear-headed enough to appreciate that if you carry socialism to its logical conclusion, you arrive at communism sooner or later.
My time is passing quickly, but I cannot forbear from reading the observations of Aubrey Jones, who wrote in the National Review in February last what I think was a penetrating analysis of socialism. He says this:
It is true that democratic socialism is not communism; in many respects, however, it is a pale reflection of it and in these non-Christian respects it also contributes to an undermining of spiritual wholesomeness and integrity. Socialism, like communism, holds out a certain extravagance of expectation; things, it is said, will be so much better when once the system is changed. That is a non-Christian trait. For the essence of Christianity is to teach, as far as this mortal sinful world is concerned, a sobriety of expectation and to affirm that great changes are brought about, not by new systems, which in fact always take on the character of old systems, but by a new spirit. That this extravagance of expectation has over a period of years been induced in England is fairly evident; it has become one of the greatest obstacles to national rehabilitation, it prevents the needed psychological adjustment to the changed national status, and through the impatience and irresponsibility to which it gives rise it bodes ill for freedom.
Again, democratic socialism, like communism, indicts a class; evil is not something common to all men, it is the badge of the capitalist; the workers, by contrast, are of superior virtue, but are held down despite themselves. This equally is not a trait of Christian belief. Nor is there anything more calculated to make class divisions permanent than this portrayal of one class as inherently better than another. It is an attitude which the wiser and soberer members among the workers themselves will wish to repudiate. Yet again, democratic socialism, like communism, sees a man's views as determined, not by a sincere quest for truth, but by his economic status. This, too, is no part of Christian belief and is conspiring to make men deaf to all honest preaching. Finally, democratic socialism, like communism, is not inspired by unselfishness; animated in very large part by rancour against the capitalist, against the man who wishes to better himself and his immediate kin, it threatens to push the state far into individual and family privacy.
The Budget-Mr. Fleming

I just wish to comment briefly in passing on one or two items in this budget. In the first place, this budget does not bring relief to the gold industry. At the present time that industry is dying. The subsidy which was provided for in this house a few weeks ago is helping only a few mines. In a large section of the gold mining areas, such as Kirkland Lake and others, there is unemployment on a large scale. This situation is attributable directly to the determination of this government to hold the Canadian dollar at an artificial level and to peg gold at an artificially low price, while the cost of the production of gold increases.
As to the increase in the interest rate on arrears of taxes, I have this to say. It is nothing short of brutally unfair on the part of the government to raise the interest rate on arrears when very often these impositions of interest are attributable directly to delay on the part of the Department of National Revenue in making the assessment. I have here a return brought down in the house recently by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) in reply to certain questions I asked. I asked the number of income tax returns not assessed as at December 31, 1947, throughout Canada. The number given in this return is 2,336,879 as of December 31 last. I would ask hon. members to note these figures. For 1943 and prior years there were 44,000-1 am just giving the round figures now-in 1944, 110,000; in 1945, 265,000; and in 1946, 1,905,000. Since that time another two million returns for the year 1947 have been filed. In the majority of cases these people do not know that they are in arrears until the assessment is made, and it is grossly unfair to heap upon them the burden of increased interest charges.
I wish to say quite definitely and, I hope, constructively, in my concluding remarks that the proposals of the Progressive Conservative party as to what this budget ought to have contained-and still ought to contain, if this government is not too stubborn-are the following. We say, first, that the budget ought to bring about a substantial reduction in indirect taxes in order to effect a decrease in the cost of living. Second, the budget should effect at once increases in the exemptions on account of income tax. Third, the whole problem of making budgets in this country should be approached from what we say is the proper point of view, namely, let the people enjoy the fruits of their labour; let them enjoy the incentive that comes from the retention of that which they have earned. That will make for increased production That alone will defeat inflation. Fourth, we

say the time has come when this government should-yes, must-reconvene the dominion-provincial conference. The need of that is apparent on every hand.
On May 14 we heard in the house the announcement of some limited assistance for the provinces, in respect of public health, but there is still no comprehensive system of social security. Nothing of that kind was attempted in those proposals, and we shall not have that until the dominion takes the responsibility for reconvening the dominion-provincial conference. In the second place, there has been no attempt to co-ordinate the public investment plans of the dominion and the provinces. In the third place, the time is ripe for reconvening the dominion-provincial conference because some of the difficulties have been removed in the form of indirect taxes.
Hon. members will recall what an important part was played in 1946 by the objections of the provinces to the continuation of the dominion in the field of indirect taxation and the difficulty that presented to the conference. They will remember the position taken by the Premier of Nova Scotia with respect to those indirect taxes. There were six of them, namely, the gasoline tax, the amusement tax, the pari-mutuel tax, the electricity tax, the security transfer tax and succession duties. The dominion has now withdrawn from four of those fields and has reduced one other of the six.
I say the time has now come when the dominion government must reconvene that conference. Canada requires it. This government need not any longer think it can bring Ontario and Quebec to their knees in a contest of attrition and nerves. I call upon this government to abandon the cold war it 'has declared against the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Let this government and the governments in all the provinces meet together like Canadians. Let this government measure up to its responsibilities and reconvene that conference. The responsibility rests upon this government.
It is a sample of the high-handed attitude of the government that when the Minister of Finance announced withdrawal from these two fields of indirect taxation, namely the amusement tax and pari-mutuel betting tax-fields which from time immemorial have been possessed by the provinces-he had this to say to the provinces, as reported at page 4068 of Hansard:
May I be permitted here to express the hope that in these cases where the dominion govern-

The Budget-Mr. J. E. Matthews
ment removes taxes of this kind and withdraws from the field, the taxpayers of Canada will receive the benefit of such action and that, so far as possible, provincial taxing authorities will refrain from stepping in.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he mind his own affairs in this federal field, and leave the provincial governments to manage theirs.
This is my final word. The policy of the Progressive Conservative party is to work unceasingly for a reduction in the load of taxation, not just a token reduction, but a substantial reduction of taxation. The policy of this government on the other hand is to continue to soak the people. The policy of the C.C.F. is to fasten upon the people of Canada the manacles of a regimented economy. The policy of the Liberal party, as declared through this government, is to surrender to those who espouse the cause of the managed economy. The Progressive Conservative party, Mr. Speaker, believes that the people are entitled and are able to manage their own affairs without paternalistic and officious intrusion into those affairs by an all-powerful Ottawa bureaucracy.
We say to this government: Get your hands out of the pockets of the people 1 Stop this plundering of the taxpayers under the guise of taxation!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not imagine I shall be expected to agree with all the remarks so forcefully made by the hon. member (Mr. Fleming) who has just taken his seat. I must admit I agree with some of what he has said. And I trust, when I have concluded what I have to say, he may also agree with some of the statements I make. I hope that to be so, even though it does not develop into a complete love feast between us.
Contrary to the hon. member's remarks, I have been impressed this year, as indeed I was a year ago, with the able budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and I wish to add my hearty congratulations to the many he has already received. I look back to the night a year ago when the present minister announced a surplus for 1946 of 8374,000,000, and a reduction in our national debt for that year of 8352,000,000.
I well recall the criticism directed against him at that time-first, because there was a surplus at all, and, second, because he had reduced our debt. My own opinion was that when the Minister of Finance at that time estimated a surplus of 8190,000,000 on this year's transactions he would not be far out. I had a lot of confidence in his cool, careful 5849-275J
calculations. But had he a year ago estimated a surplus of, not $190,000,000 but 8670,000,000, my faith in his judgment would have received a severe shock.
I do not propose to follow this debate through all the devious channels it may pursue. To me, one acid test of the year's transactions is that the business of Canada has been kept going under a full head of steam. In some instances taxes have been reduced-not very much; and $670,000,000 has been paid on our national debt.
Critics may talk for months on the smaller questions involved; but again I say that the huge reduction in our debt is the acid test and cannot be controverted. There was the $352,000,000 reduction in 1946 and $647,000,000 in 1947, making about a billion dollars of our national debt paid in two years.
How will that affect our interest payments for the coming year? Well, the interest on a billion dollars at three per cent would be $30,000,000 a year. That $30,000,000 saving each year may appear just chicken feed to some; but it is not so to me. It may be well to keep in mind that for eighty-one years, since confederation, the federal government has had only seventeen surpluses. They were in 1871, i872, 1900, 1903, 1904, 1907, 1912, 1913, 1924 to 1930, 1947 and 1948.
It is safe to assume that the two last-mentioned outdistance all former surpluses combined. We should also not forget that our Minister of Finance has an unbroken record of surpluses, one for every year he has occupied the driver's seat. Not only that, but he estimates another half billion surplus for. 1948; and I say, "More power to him."
To me a nation's business, so far as the finances are concerned, is the business of the individuals who comprise that nation. The taxpayers of Canada are the shareholders of this huge government business. We have a general manager, and he has presented his annual report called the budget speech. The question which interests me most, and which should interest every shareholder-otherwise called taxpayer-is whether or not our general manager, known as the Minister of Finance, and those associated with him, are making a success of their work.
I suggest that a general manager of any business in the world who could show results to his shareholders comparable with those reported by the Minister of Finance in his annual report would be wined and dined as the hero of the company. The shareholders without exception would be proud of him, and their applause would not take the form of a want of confidence motion.
Such a motion means only this, that he should be replaced by some new, untried and

The Budget-Mr. J. E. Matthews
possibly inexperienced amateur. I can assure my good friends that the people of Canada, the shareholders of our nation's business, are not so gullible as to take on any such risk as that. The shareholders will be inclined to ask definitely, who is in mind, anyway, to succeed the Minister of Finance. I wonder how many people in Canada realize that if you take all the railways of Canada and all the chartered banks of Canada and tie them all up together, their combined business as indicated by gross revenue is only one-third of the volume of business transacted by the dominion government. That is to say, the gross revenue of all the railways of Canada is $758 million, and of all the banks of Canada, $229 million, and of the dominion government $2,869 million, or three times greater.
The cost of running this huge business last year, for instance, was $1,985 million; and at that it was $131 million less than the previous year. May I emphasize here a statement made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, that a total of $1,214,288,000 of Canada's expenditures is uncontrollable-such items as family allowances, pensions, interest on the public debt, subsidies for provinces, contributions to various government agencies. My criticism is-and I shall be frank about it- that what are called "uncontrollable expenditures" have been permitted to reach proportions far beyond what is reasonable or necessary in this country. These uncontrollable expenditures had better be kept under control. It is the taxpayer's money. He proposes to have a voice as to how that money will be spent. I think in that regard a word to the wise might be sufficient.
I have not much respect for an individual who does not pay his bills, or at least make an effort to do so. I have the deepest sympathy for the man who, because of ill-health or unavoidable losses, cannot discharge his indebtedness. My feelings toward a nation are exactly the same as toward an individual.
I have no hesitation in saying that the minister has a sound idea in reducing our indebtedness each year to the largest possible degree now, when times are good. You may call it cyclical budgeting, if you wish, but I call it plain, common sense. Taxes are never popular, but the real test is not how much taxes you have paid, but how much you have remaining after they are paid.
I shall not take the time to speak of fishing, mining, pulpwood production and many other sources of revenue, but at this time I want to make special reference to agriculture. So far as I am aware, Canada has never had a Minister of Agriculture who has worked so zealously and so persistently in the interests 
of the farmer as has the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I say that quite frankly and I do not think anyone will attempt to contradict me. He had the vision to see, and the government had the vision to support him, that a prosperous farm population would contribute immeasurably to the prosperity of Canada as a whole and therefore make this country better able to bear the tremendous financial demands resulting from the war.
To that end he set his course, with the result that, during the years 1939 to 1947 inclusive, there was paid to farmers in Canada in subsidies, bonuses, freight assistance and other similar forms, no less than $528,979,000. That is a lot of money over and above the regular farm income. That amount includes bonus cheques which farmers received on quality cheese amounting to approximately $12,000,000; on fluid and concentrated milk, butter-fats, et cetera, $156,000,000. The premium on hogs amounted to $35,000,000. Then there were other channels, including $87,000,000 which was applied to prairie farm assistance in the form of acreage bonuses resulting from poor crops; there was $25,000,000 for prairie farm rehabilitation to build dams, dug-outs and other conservation works; there was $19,000,000 prairie farm income, including such items as compensation for storing grain on the farm; there was $88,000,000 for wheat acreage reduction, which means just what it says. Then $100,000,000 was applied to feed freight assistance, feed wheat drawbacks, plus over $2,000,000 subsidy to increase Canada's bacon export trade, along with another $1,000,000 as an egg export subsidy.
I suggest that there had to be a lot of cheques issued in Ottawa and cashed by the farmers of Canada to absorb the tremendous amounts I have quoted. Someone will ask whether these huge payments have been justified, but my answer will be that they have been amply justified, away beyond the slightest contradiction. Farmers and non-farmers felt that the cash farm return in 1946 of $1,752,000,000 might not be equalled for many years, it being twice as high as it was in 1939.
But what happened? The returns for 1947 showed an increase of $237,900,000 over 1946, or a total of $1,990,600,000, or close to the two billion mark. In other words, there was an increase of $161,000,000 over Canada's previous peak year of 1944. The 1947 farm income that I have quoted includes an increase over 1946 of $128,000,000 from the sale of grain, seed and hay; and an increase from the sale of livestock from $574,600,000 in 1946 to $590,000,000 in 1947. But it does not include payments made to farmers under the Prairie Farm

The Budget-Mr. J. E. Matthews
Assistance Act, another $11,577,000, this bringing the total farm income last year to the astounding figure of $2,002,000,000. Two billion dollars-we may well wonder, along with the Minister of Agriculture, when and to what extent that record will ever be broken.
It was illuminating, to say the least, to read in a western paper not long ago a letter signed C. Bolton, Knighton, Radnorshipe, England, paying wonderful tribute to Canada's Minister of Agriculture, a9 "a man of vision", something, he said, which was very much lacking in the world today. "He wisely agreed," said Mr. Bolton, "to a wheat price which he knew we could pay, and which over a series of years would undoubtedly pay the farmers, for whom he works so hard, much better than an inflated price and a defaulting creditor." Mr. Bolton goes on to express some comparisons so striking that it would be scarcely ethical to quote them here.
So far as 1948 is concerned, the twenty cents a bushel increase in the initial wheat payment, retroactive for three crops, will put many a farmer away to another good start, meaning, as it does, the distribution of an extra $150,000,000 now being made among western farmers. The return this year also of the refundable portions, the compulsory saving feature, of the 1943 and 1944 income taxes, amounting to $230,000,000, will bring revenue into many homes, besides reducing future interest payments by the government.
As against this, however, there are extra expenditures to be provided for. The new health program is placed at an initial annual expenditure of $30,000,000 a year. The increase in Canada's war pensions will boost that expenditure from $73,000,000 to $91,000,000 per year. This commendable increase will benefit 400,000 Canadian men, women and children, including 153,000 disabled veterans and 17,000 widows.
The increase in old age pensions, pensions for the blind, health and hospitalization allowances and more persons drawing family allowances, will mean another $27,000,000 expenditure for 1948. These expenditures, along with unemployment insurance, war service gratuities, and similar grants, have increased tremendously during the past ten years. For instance, the amount paid in family allowances since its inception is around $700,000,000.
I have quoted sufficient to indicate that the farmers as a whole all across Canada have made a wonderful response in the matter of production. There have been references of late to the butter supply. Some claimed that the farmers, particularly the younger farmers, were letting the country down in dairy production. I did not believe it, at all events so far as Manitoba is concerned. In order to settle the point, I have before me the official report issued by the department of agriculture of Manitoba. From that report I learn that creamery butter manufactured in Manitoba in 1947 amounted to 26,265,141 pounds or an increase of 198,513 pounds over 1946; and dairy butter, 5,963,000 pounds.
The total milk production in Manitoba in 1947 was 1,230,740,429 pounds, or an increase of 11,666,792 pounds over 1946. There were seventy creameries manufacturing butter in Manitoba in 1947, and twenty-three manufacturing cheese. The estimated farm value of butter, creamery and dairy, made in Manitoba last year was $14,534,000, and of cheese, $890,000.
The total farm value of the milk produced in that province was $25,932,000. I mention these figures to show that if there is any slowing down of milk production in Canada, the fault cannot be laid at the door of Manitoba farmers.
In hog production the number of carcasses shipped in 1947 was less than in 1946; the number of live hogs remaining on the farm at the end of 1947 was more.
May I add right here, as a matter of information, that the official report from which I have quoted gives the following estimated average income per farm as follows:
Average
Year	per farm
1941		 $1,550

1943		 3,040
1944		 3,444
1945		 2,779
1946		 3,416
1947		 3,597
When speaking on the budget a year ago, I referred, perhaps boastfully, to the success of Manitoba farmers at the Toronto Royal all down the years, and particularly in 1946. Last November, or was it December, they even eclipsed all former records. They exhibited 128 animals and won 135 prizes, including twenty-two firsts, twenty-five seconds, nineteen thirds, sixteen fourths, thirteen fifths, eleven sixths, and the remainder in close proximity. In addition to prizes, they won outstanding awards, namely two grand championships, two reserve grand, one senior, one reserve senior, one junior, five reserve juniors. In 1946, they won eleven awards and ninety-eight prizes; in 1947, twelve awards and 135 prizes. No further comment is necessary regarding the excellence of Manitoba livestock.
This good farming and attention to business has brought commendable results. For instance,

The Budget-Mr. J. E. Matthews
last year the Manitoba farm loans association had only 310 outstanding mortgages, 303 agreements for sale, and 193 farms remaining for settlement, as against 1,162 mortgages, 657 agreements for sale, and 641 farms in 1941. The association's collections last year alone approached the million dollar mark.
The record of the Canadian farm loan board is equally good. Of 1,678 first mortgages and 222 second mortgages, the amount of principal overdue more than six months at the end of 1947 was $65.71, and the amount of interest overdue, not one dollar.
A writer in an American magazine not long ago deplored the unscientific methods of Canadian agriculture. I read the article to the end, expecting to find some explanation as to why Canadian farmers took the first ten places in the world wheat competition at Chicago in 1947. I expected to find some explanation as to wrhy Canadian farmers almost invariably win the grand championships in wheat, barley and oats in American competitions, and as to why the most advanced American farmers grow, though not so successfully, the finer sturdier varieties of wheat, developed by Canadian scientists. I did lot find the explanation.
Speaking of progress made by many western farmers, I want to draw attention to an organization that quietly and without ostentation has been doing very effective work in this country. I refer to the Farm Improvement Loans Act passed in 1944 during the financial administration of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). The act was designed as a short cut to the more speedy financing of improvements on the farm. The loans were actually made through the chartered banks, but with a substantial degree of government endorsation. They were put through at five per cent interest, and during the three years 1945-46-47 approximately forty thousand farmers obtained loans, amounting to thirty-one and a half million dollars, for the purpose of farm and home improvements.
It is interesting to note to what wise and helpful uses these loans were approximately applied.
Thirty thousand loans ($25,000,000) were applied to the purchase of farm implements, notably trucks and tractors.
Four thousand loans (over $4,000,000) were for the construction or repair of farm dwellings, bams and outbuildings.
Twenty-five hundred loans (almost $1,000,000) were for the clearing and breaking of new land, resulting in 123,680 acres heretofore uncultivated having been brought into production. Seventeen hundred and twentyfive loans (over $1,000,000) were applied to the purchase of livestock.
One hundred and forty-nine loans ($86,000) were devoted to fencing and farm drainage.
Better still, although operations were begun only in 1945, nearly half the loans made up to the end of 1947 have already been repaid in full, notwithstanding the fact that loans may be effected for a period up to ten years.
Thus far, not one dollar loss has been experienced, a record which speaks volumes for the wise and efficient administration of the act. The fact also that approximately 40,000 Canadian farm homes have already been made more comfortable, or the farm rendered more productive, as a result of those loans, is ample justification of the recent extension of the act for another three years. I submit that this type of legislation is desirable and constructive and has the added virtue of being in no sense paternalistic.
We may well wonder if, and when, the pendulum may begin to swing the other way; for it would seem improbable that our present successes will continue indefinitely without reverses of some kind. It is assuring, however, to note the efforts toward stabilizing conditions that are being made. For instance, what a hopeful statement was that made by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) recently when he announced that 4,000 Canadian companies will invest a billion and a half dollars before March 31, 1949, in a reconversion program producing new commodities in Canada. Hon. members will admit that this is facing the situation in the minister's characteristic big way.
Then again, the recent international wheat agreement endorsed by thirty-six importing and exporting nations, after several years' efforts, is an achievement which Canada has long sought.
Many former markets are now non-existent, and have to be replaced. To this end, in formulating international trade agreements- thus expanding in ever-widening circles our business relations with other countries-Canada owes a big debt to the recent Minister of Trade and Commerce, the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacKinnon). I am confident that few people realize how great is the contribution he has made to expanding the trade of this country. For instance, last year's substantial increase in trade was augmented by an increase in our exports to Latin American countries of over 50 per cent, those to Argentina showing an increase of almost 200 per cent; in fact, almost every republic in South and Central America has increased its Canadian buying. Canadian exports also to Australia and New Zealand are reported to have

The Budget-Mr. J. E. Matthews
increased about 80 per cent over 1946. Our exports to Brazil, which used to amount to about five million dollars, grew in 1946 to
824,600,000.
Canada was the second largest source of supply for Britain last year, with an increase of 17 per cent over 1946.
As hon. members are aware, the former Minister of Trade and Commerce made an extensive trip last year and, I think, proved himself a splendid combination of salesman and statesman. No one can estimate what that one trip will mean to the future trade of this country. I desire to quote briefly from an article in the Monetary Times in which the former Minister of Trade and Commerce gives his own impressions.
As head of the Canadian trade mission to South Africa and the Mediterranean area, it was my privilege to share personally in yet another constructive step towards the promotion of Canadian trade. Travelling some 25,000 miles, the mission, made up of prominent Canadian industrialists and government officials, visited eleven different countries for trade discussions, and touched briefly at seven others. Our primary object was a good will visit to Canada's third best customer, the Union of South Africa, which is more fortunate than other sterling countries in that she is able to pay for dollar imports out of her vast gold resources. Everywhere the mission travelled it met with a reception which could leave no doubt with respect to the warm regard in which Canada is held abroad. Officials and businessmen alike were impressed by the fact that we had a genuine interest in trying to assist them in developing a market in Canada for their products, as well as in promoting our own export trade. The good will resulting from the visits made by the mission will be remembered for many years, and I am sure wi11 ^ have a most beneficial effect on Canada's trading relations in the future.
We hear a great deal today about the cost of living. I was interested in an article published on May 3, 1947, by the London Recorder, giving a breakdown of how the average man and woman in England spent each pound of personal expenditure in 1946. I have the list before me, and I have translated the amounts into terms of dollar spending, to make it more readily understandable here. These are the figures for England, out of each dollar of personal expenditure, as I have stated:

It will surprise many Canadians to learn
from a statement made by the minister that in the United States a single taxpayer with no dependents has exemption up to only $600; and that, while in Canada $800 means an income tax of $5, in the United States it means a tax of $20; also that a married taxpayer with no children has exemption in the United States up to only $1,200. In Canada a $1,600 income means to such a person a tax of $10, but in the United States a tax of $40.
I stand four square in support of the government in having had the will and the courage to impose taxes commensurate with the imperative demands of war. This is no time for our Canadian people to forget the astounding contribution made by this country toward prosecution of the war. And why not? It was our war, and upon the result of that war depended our freedom, with all that word involves. Yes, our war effort was stupendous, and the taxes we are paying today, as a result of that war effort, are, and will continue to be, a definite burden. Yet, in terms of what we have remaining, our contribution is a mere bagatelle when compared with the devastated homes and absolute ruin visited upon our allied nations in Europe.
Furthermore, I am confident it can never be said that Canada scuttled the allied ship with the cessation of hostilities. Our nearest ally should be better versed on that score than any other nation, and it is encouraging, yes, inspiring, to read in some United States papers acknowledgment of Canada's contribution to post-war efforts. At Washington recently the

The Budget-Mr. J. E. Matthews
Tabloid News paid tribute to what our country has done in the way of aid to Europe, stating that Canada's aid in terms of relative population or national income is greater than that of the United States. These are its concluding words:
To the world's need in peace or war, Canada makes a bold and sacrificial contribution, but quietly and without fanfare.
The Portland, Oregon, Journal, in a fairly recent article pointed out that Canada's population is only one-eleventh of the United States, and her national income about one-fifteenth, so that the loans and outright gifts of 81,850 million made by Canada to Europe are the equivalent of a United States loan of 820,350 million in terms of population, or $27,750 million in terms of national income. Surely this is a striking comparison and a friendly tribute from our southern neighbour.
These facts have been widely commented upon by other leading papers in the United States. I could quote from many others did time permit. For instance, the New York World-Telegram, with a daily circulation of almost 400,000, has this to say concerning the facts I have cited:
It is a sturdy and noble people that we have to the north of us. Canadians are a bulwark of democracy and decency. We are indeed fortunate in our neighbours.
Mr. Speaker, I would commend those words from United States papers to some hon. members in this chamber who never lose an opportunity of endeavouring to belittle Canada whether in war or peace.
We sometimes hear it said that all that portion of a taxpayer's income exceeding $25,000 should be confiscated. Well, that would not help very much. A concise analysis appeared in an Ottawa paper not long ago, bearing upon 1946 returns:
The figures showed that the combined incomes of all Canadians getting $25,000 a year or more totalled $113 million. If, therefore, the government were to take away from this group every cent they made, it would still be short about $1,600 million of what it needs in the way of cash in order to administer the country. If put in another way, all the incomes of all our so-called rich, grabbed by Mr. Abbott, wouldn't be enough to pay half of the baby bonus for one year.
The people of Canada may expect to pay taxes, heavy taxes, for many years as a result of the war. So long as those taxes are applied in substantial measure to reduce our national debt, Canadians will take a reasonable view of the situation. But they are going to insist, yes, they are going to demand, and I hope they will, that the taxes which they pay and for which they have worked

so hard are not frittered away in fantastic government expenditures.
Even with the astounding reductions in our national debt made during the past two years by the Minister of Finance, we are still burdened with a debt of enormous proportions. It seems to me that in order to retire that debt we must have millions more people in Canada. We must open our doors more widely than ever before to desirable immigrants from other countries. We have a tremendous extent of country populated by only twelve million people. Europe, including Britain, with an area half the size of Canada, has a population of four hundred million. In other words, were we as densely peopled as Europe, our population would be eight hundred million instead of only twelve million. We have a task before us. We cannot expect to hold indefinitely great stretches of unoccupied lands when there are many million human beings huddled together in other countries, yearning to assist in the development of Canada's rich and, to a large extent, untouched resources. Yes, a largely increased population will be a potent factor in the reduction of our national debt.
As regards taxation, some resentment was engendered among farmers with respect to the new income tax forms prepared for 1947 returns. I believe that to quite an extent, particularly in western Canada, the object, or what I hope was the object, of that new form was misunderstood.
I am glad to endorse the new efforts made by the department to run down tax evaders. Honest taxpayers all across Canada will heartily endorse that action.
I cannot recall having heard at any session so many members lauding their constituencies, and at considerable length, as during the present session. It was all very commendable, all very interesting, and I think we should have more of it.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say all honour to those who have not hesitated to place on the record of this parliament a tribute to the constituencies they represent, and to the efforts of the people.
However, I am in a position to pay a tribute greater still to the people of my constituency, and one not touched upon by other members. We have it on the highest authority that life does not consist of bread alone, and that a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches. Let me say here that I have the honor and the satisfaction of representing the constituency of Brandon in the House of Commons longer, with one exception, than any member since confederation. And in all those years, it has never

The Budget-Mr. H. 0. White
been suggested to me directly or indirectly that I should stoop to any political act of a doubtful nature. That is my tribute to my constituents, and it is one of which I am justly proud.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I again congratulate the minister and his department on a big task having been carried to a successful conclusion by a big man.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising tonight to discuss the budget I must say that, after hearing the Minister of Finance present it the other night,
I more or less came to the conclusion that I would not take part in the debate because there was not much in the budget to inspire an address of any kind. It did not present any incentives to those in labour, industry or farming to increase production, and we as a free-enterprise countiy must offer something besides the rvhip if we are to increase production.
I would point out to my socialist friends to the left that there are no other twelve million people in the world who have produced as much food and sent abroad munitions of war to the same extent as the twelve million Canadians have done.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is
right, and under free enterprise too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to say a word or two about the way in which the budget affects my own constituency, and as it affects my constituency so also will it affect the Canadian people. Taxation is discouraging production. I only need to refer to a couple of items to bring that home to the house. One is reduction in the production of cheese and the other is hogs.
I have in my hand two editorials, one from the Ottawa Journal and the other from the London Free Press, both dealing with food problems. One deals with the statement of Sir John Boyd Orr a few days ago, and the editorial comment of the Ottawa Journal on his statements. The other is a report in the London Free Press on the agricultural institute of Canada meeting in Guelph on June 23 next.
Sir John Boyd Orr points out the vast increase in the population of the world. It is 40,000,000 since Y-E day. James Turner, of the world federation of farmers, has pointed out that in 1951 production of food will be only the same as in 1939; yet by that time there will be more of an increase than the
40,000,000 in the population of the world. And these 40,000,000 did not bring one acre of ground with them on which to produce more food.
I think we as Canadians can produce a good deal more food than we have; but you cannot get the Canadian farmer, or labour or industiy to produce at a loss for long, and therefore I want to point out to the government just how this is affecting a good many people.
Of all the things that are bothering the farmers, labour and small business, income tax is, in my opinion, the worst. I have talked to a good many farmers and they are quite prepared to pay their share of income tax if they owe it. Labour and the salaried worker never get a chance to handle their share because it is taken away from them before they get it, and so they see to it that they only work so long and do not get into the higher income brackets. The result is that they will lay off for a day or two, so that there is a decrease in production all across the board. If some means could be found of reducing the burden of income tax, or if those exemptions in the lower income brackets could be raised, so that people generally could have some relief, they would be able to buy food, and it would be a relief to those producing food. They would have an incentive to produce more, so that the consumer could get it at more reasonable cost.
I was quite interested in this article with reference to Sir John Boyd Orr, because in all the plans that are being made there has been no mention of rewarding the man who produces food. I can say to that organization and to the agricultural institute that until they take into consideration the man who is going to produce the food, and the necessity of rewarding him, they will not get the food and they might as well cease their deliberations. If they think the farmer will work for nothing and board himself they will be disillusioned people.
We did not ask labour during the war to give its services for practically nothing, nor did we ask industry to do so. We rewarded industry and labour and they produced the sinews of war and were enabled to produce them in abundance. We can do the same again as far as food is concerned, but the farmer will not do it for nothing.
The other evening one of our socialist members, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr, Nicholson), I believe, was mentioning the need for subsidized housing, and he went so far as to say that we should have subsidized farm housing. I submit that if any group of people are adequately rewarded or paid they can provide their own housing, whether in the city or in the country. But what has happened? Under subsidized housing, the farmer, and every citizen in the land who has paid for
The Budget-Mr. H. 0. White

his own home, or is paying for it, will be asked to provide a home for some improvident person, without thrift or regard for the future, who wants someone to pay for a home for him. That is what subsidized housing means. You and I will pay for someone else's home.

speechtext:
Let me say that there are many vacant houses in the country, but people do not want to work at jobs that are necessary where these houses are. These houses are on the farms, and that is a good indication that the man who tills the soil is not being rewarded, in relation to the hours of work he puts in, and the knowledge and ability he must put into -that work. Those people who think food is too dear will find many farms in Middlesex county that can be bought for the price of a house and lot in the city, and they will not be out of a job if they go there. They will have food at cost, but I will not tell them What that cost is. They know it just as well as I do, and they do not want to go there.
We hear quite a bit about stabilization of farm prices, the price of farm products, and that sounds good to a lot of people. But it does not take a great deal of ability to stabilize the prices of farm products below the world price or below parity price, and the recent moves on the part of consumers demanding the admission of oleomargarine into the country are a fair indication that the consumers will not stand for higher prices if the world price should drop below levels which the consuming public can afford to pay. They will not stand for it now and they certainly will not stand for it in the future. I think we are just holding out a hope to the farmers that when things are not so good, the prices of their products will be higher. That is certainly just a dream and nothing else.

The other evening the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) speaking on the plight of the farmer, was bemoaning -the fact that the average income of the farmer was less than that of any of the other groups in Canada. But I notice that the hon. member for Skeena and all the other members of his group voted for the wheat bill which gave the farmer less than -the world price. I also notice that they voted for the agricultural bill to put coarse grains under the wheat act. So it seems to me -that they are inconsistent. They talk on the one hand about the fact that the farmer is not getting enough for his produce, and yet they vote the other way when the opportunity arises.
Recently the dominion bureau of statistics provided these figures. The labour income index in Canada in the last -twelve months has risen forty-four points, while the farm income index has receded fourteen points. How do we arrive at that? It is because most of th-e things the farmer has to buy have increased in price -to a greater extent than -the things the farmer has to sell. So we find ourselves in that particular plight at the moment.
What else has the budget done or not done that my constituents do not like? One of them is this. The tax on soft drinks and candies is not removed. Workers and children are usually the buyers of those products. On the other hand, the tax on pari-mutuel betting, which aids a group of people that are not greatly in need of aid, was removed. So I say that the government was unwise in that particular move.
Actually the budget was not brought down last week; it was brought down on November 17 last when a twenty-five per cent increase in excise taxes were placed on many articles that the low income groups have to buy. When that tax was put on, it gave the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) the opportunity to say at this time that he had built up a huge surplus and that he was not increasing taxation in any lines, but was able to reduce taxation in a few. If you can put on a heavy tax five or six months before the budget comes down, and then say you have taken off some here and some there, it may sound good at the moment; but as far as the people back home are concerned, they are still digging down in their pockets and paying to this government in taxes thirty-three cents out of every dollar they receive. So I would say that, as far as my people are concerned they are disappointed.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
The only bright part of the budget is the fact that the minister was able to reduce the national debt. I want to point out again-
I have said it before in this house, and I am going to say it again-that we, our children and our children's children will be paying for subsidized food that was supplied to people who were more able to buy it during the war years than they will ever be in the years to come. So when you hear people asking for subsidies, you know they are wanting somebody else to pay for something they want, and that somebody else is you.
I repeat again, Mr. Speaker, that the budget was a dismal disappointment. It was a budget of sixty-five or die. I think the amendment of the Progressive Conservative party was absolutely in order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister's budget speech, Mr. Speaker, is one more budget speech of despair. It contains no hint of any new order of abundance and freedom such as our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) promised us all during the war. We find in it no sign of any brave new world worth fighting for. It is a budget of privation, scarcity and frustration. Why was the budget such a chilling disappointment? It seems to me that the people of Canada ought to know. They realize that in Canada we have a magnificent heritage, with an abundance of resources of almost every kind; a wonderful people, skillful, aggressive, buoyant, able and ready to work. Yet we have to have conditions such as this budget imposes on us. Why is this?
The answer is that this budget is based on an oxcart financial system trying to function in an age of internal combustion engines; in fact in an age of jet propulsion. Small wonder it fails to do the job!
There is but little comfort to be found in the speech of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) who, I presume, would be preparing the budget speech if the Conservatives were in power.
