speechtext:
They everlastingly
talk about getting to the stars, but they have not the slightest idea of how to get their feet out of the mud on the earth.
The present orthodox financial system simply must be changed. Let that be borne in upon every member of the house and upon every person in the country. Just as long as we persist in keeping the present orthodox financial system, we shall have budget after budget of the type of that which we have just had presented to us.
There will be those who will wonder if there is any evidence to support the statement that I make. I do not wish to bring myself into the limelight particularly, Mr. Speaker, but I hereby issue a challenge to the Minister of Finance and the members of the Liberal and Conservative parties to debate the fundamental principles of finance. I defy any one of them to prove that the Canadian nation has to finance entirely with debt money. I will give them all the time they need to prepare themselves, and when they are ready to come, I will be ready. We are financing this nation, and have been ever since some time in the middle of the first world war, with debt money. The debt money idea is part of the general mentality of scarcity which apparently prevails universally among Liberals and Conservatives throughout the country. The budget at the present time proposes to finance all Canadian activities with debt.
The one bright spot thus far in the budget debate is the Social Credit speech of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). I do not wish to slight the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He merely told what was wrong in some respects with the budget; he did not tell us how the wrong could be made right.
The Social Credit proposals, in brief, were as follows-and I shall make a summary of them so that we shall have them before us. It was proposed that we have a national monetary authority responsible to parliament and vested with power in the name of the people of Canada to enable those things which are physically possible and desirable to be made financially possible. As an initial step in a comprehensive debt retirement program the monetary authority to call upon the chartered banks to surrender to the Bank of Canada three and a half to four billion dollars of pappajo oq 0} spreq qong; *sopi.inoas uoimmop

on the books of the Bank of Canada with the face value of the securities delivered, this credit to be an asset to balance the liabilities of the bank to its depositors.
The national monetary authority so to regulate the use of this credit as to enable the chartered banks to meet the liabilities to their depositors in an orderly fashion, and in a manner to maintain the stability of the national economy.
Third, cancellation of existing reduction in family allowances for each child after the fourth as the first step toward an ultimate increase of fifty per cent in all family allowance, costing $15,000,000.
Immediate old age pensions of $50 at seventy years of age without a means test; the first step toward an objective of $50 at sixty-an additional $169,000,000.
Pensions for needy widows at sixty years of age and over and payments to all disabled adults not otherwise provided for by government allowances, eighteen years of age and over $20,000,000 additional.
Provision for increasing war veterans allowances to $50 and $85 a month for single and married persons respectively, and to increase 100 per cent disability to $100 a month, an additional $10,000,000.
Provision for encouragement by subsidy or otherwise increased production of such things as sugar, coal and Steel to make Canada selfsufficient and to save American dollars- $75,000,000.
Abolition of the salles tax, $395,000,000; accompanied by measures to ensure benefits to consumers.
Cancellation of the recently imposed excise tax of 25 per cent.
Income tax exemptions to be raised to $1,500 and $2,400 as an initial step in ultimate exemptions of $2,000 and $3,000 respectively- $300,000,000.
Ten per cent exemption of corporate profits for income tax purposes conditional upon companies handing over the sales tax abolition benefits to consumers; the rate of tax on profits between ten and twenty per cent on capital to be at 60 per cent; tax on profits over 20 per cent to be at 80 per cent.
The total upset in the present budget would be $984,000,000, to be provided for as follows:
(a)	by using from the estimated surplus $484,000,000.
(b)	by saving in interest charges through the debt reduction, $100,000,000.
(c)	estimated increases in revenue from increased buoyancy, $100,000,000.
(d)	by national credit, $300,000,000.
One item there that might not be easy for the orthodox financial mind to understand is the

last one, the national credit of $300 million. I maintain there is some hope in that budget. The question that will from time to time be raised will be whether or not that budget is sound, whether it will actually work in the Dominion of Canada in the year 1948-49.
It will be argued that Social Credit proposals are unrealistic, unscientific and unsound. It will be contended that Social Credit proposals will cause inflation. I will argue that Social Credit proposals are realistic, scientific and sound; and I contend that Social Credit proposals will not cause inflation in a wisely managed Canada.
Social Credit proposals will not cause inflation in a wisely managed Canada, because Canada has such a tremendous amount of resources of such a wide variety and she has her industry developed to such a high degree that she is completely capable or can be made completely capable of supplying the needs of her people, or goods which she can trade for needs which we cannot supply.
The first question I ask is: What is inflation? Inflation is a rise in prices which results from a scarcity of goods. When I first came to parliament it was impossible to get any Liberal to consent to the truthfulness of that definition. But today the war has forced them all to agree that that is the definition of inflation. It is a rise in prices fundamentally brought about by a shortage of goods.
What are the causes of inflation? The first cause is a shortage of goods in relation to money in circulation. The second is taxation. It is not a real cause of inflation, but it is a cause of a rise in prices which is called inflation in the country today. The third is the increased cost of production, such as the increase in freight rates, the increase in the cost of gasoline and the like. This also is not a real cause of inflation, but it again is the cause of a rise in prices and must be counted in when determining the causes of rise in prices called inflation. The fourth cause is over-capitalization, and the fifth cause is over-exportation.
I do not propose to deal in detail with all of these. I mention them as being the main factors which are contributing to the high cost of goods prevailing in Canada today; such high costs being commonly called inflation and being blamed generally upon the fact that there is too much money in circulation for the goods in the country.
What are the safeguards against inflation- the safeguards which would be used in this Social Credit budget which the hon. member for Peace River proposes? Here are some of them. In the first place, we should stimulate our production. This has been spoken of by scores of members in the house. I think the

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
country is pretty well agreed as to how we could stimulate our production. Here are some of the proposals which all hon. members speak about rather freely.
First, remove or at least alleviate all incentive destroying factors such as, for example, discouraging taxation, which the hon. member who just took his seat was discussing;
Second, remove uncertainty of markets; Third, remove undependability of prices. These factors are within the control of our generation, if we use the facilities which are at our disposal. And we need not become a socialized state in order to use those powers.
Next, we should carefully plan, in conjunction with the provinces, definitely to make Canada self-sufficient so far as possible. We should make definitely a balanced economy, as is eloquently advocated by Mr. W. H. Moore, who was an honoured member of the house, representing the constituency of Ontario, in his fine book called "Grey Days", published in 1946, a book which I would encourage all hon. members to read.
Again, we should adopt proper protective measures to give confidence to Canadian producers. These measures which are at our disposal, and may be undoubtedly used, and which we see in operation today, are quantitative restrictions; that is, keeping out those goods which we do not want to come in to destroy the market for our own goods. For example, when we are producing tomatoes we do not want outside tomatoes supplying the market.
We can keep them out by quantitative restrictions, so far as we require to do. In addition to quantitative restrictions, we can use subsidies and we can use exchange control. These three measures could exclude outside goods entirely. If the government and the various provincial governments of the country had the courage to say, "We are going to produce in Canada, for example, our own tomatoes; we are announcing to the world we are going to and we are announcing to Canada we are going to; we invite an all-over effort to produce tomatoes; produce them and we will guarantee the Canadian market"-if something similar is done with the various commodities that 'Canada can produce so well, then the producers will rise in great numbers if they are guaranteed interesting prices and an assured market.
There is nothing unreasonable about that proposal. We should impose rationing on goods in short supply and we should grant compensated discounts on goods in plentiful supply. There is nothing new or revolutionary in either one of those proposals; they were
used freely and broadly during the war with great success and could have been used during the peace with equally great success. This last proposal, that of granting compensated discounts on goods in plentiful supply, is a means of price control. It is the price control w'hich the Social Credit organization advocates, being price control by inducement and not by compulsion.
Then we should adopt generally effective and aggressive measures to increase the production of goods essential to Canada's freedom and prosperity, such as the production of our own coal, our own steel, our own oil for fuel, our own gas, our own electricity and the other things which we can produce, including our own sugar.
Any ordinary individual looking at the way in which Canada has managed her household during the last forty-five or fifty years would be struck with absolute astonishment that a group of intelligent people should so mismanage the magnificent asset which is Canada, allowing themselves to go billions and billions of dollars into debt to outside countries for commodities which could be produced in Canada with great success if the people just set about doing it.
I should like to give an example of the injurious effects which taxation has upon production and prices. If production is impaired, if prices are allowed to rise, both bring on inflation. Consequently this example of the injurious effects of taxation will indicate how that sort of thing can work toward inflation. May I read an excerpt from a rather interesting book which has come into my hands entitled, "Lincoln's incentive system," by James F. Lincoln. This man Lincoln is head of one of the greatest companies in the world making the product he makes. His book was published only recently in 1946. What he puts into his book is the results of his own practical experience in his own magnificent company in the United States. This is what he says on page 72:
Only the consumer pays taxes in the final analysis. This statement may need clarification.
Let us take a case in point. We go to a gas station to buy a gallon of gas, for which we pay 20 cents. Of that, six cents is advertised as sales tax. That leaves 14 cents. The company providing the gas pays taxes of over 100 million dollars. Each gallon produced must pay its share of this tax which is about two cents. The railroad transported the gas. It pays another 100 million of taxes. That adds another cent in freight charge. The station that sells it has a tax which adds another cent. All the people who furnish the oil company any and all supplies, labour, or material must add their taxes in their charges, since they can get their money to pay taxes only from their customers. After all the taxes have been taken out, the gas cost

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
is Jess than four cents, the taxes nearly 16 cents. If the 16 cents Jiad been listed as sales tax we should scream our heads off. Or should we?
And then at page 138 he says:
The present graduated income tax, which excludes the possibility of the able to profit from their ability, will in the same "way that serfdom did eliminate the best efforts of the able in our economy. What is more serious, it will stop the further development of the latent abilities of those on whom -we depend for leadership in our economy. Not only that, it will kill the desire of the rising generation to develop. This, if continued, will wreck our economy if we are to meet the competition of other nations who give freedom of opportunity to their industries and their citizens.
And further on:
I wonder what our reaction to the govern-mental_ taxation would have been if, at the time of the passing of the income tax law, we had been told that this law, with its double taxation of profits and renegotiation, would take from the stockholders in many cases over 99 per cent of every dollar of profit made by the industry.
Perhaps that would be excused by the statement "that can happen only to the rich stockholder who gets too much anyway." How should we have reacted if we had known that a widovr, whose sole income was from 100 shares of stock of the Lincoln Electric Company, was to be taxed 95 per cent on her part of the profit of the company? Out of $12,000 of company profit, the government took $11,400 and left her $600. Still more important, a large part of the $11,400 taken from her by the government would have gone to the consumer in lower prices, had not government grabbed it out of her hand.
That is a rather striking account of the effect of income tax on production and prices in the United States. I would imagine that if a carefully prepared statement were made in Canada it would be just as revealing as that one.
May I give now an example of the relatively simple means which we could adopt to bring about an improvement in the Canadian production of coal. May I quote from an address by Mervyn Brown on a national coal policy at a parliamentary dinner on April 28, 1948. Many hon. members will remember that. He said:
The extensive report made by the Milnes Coal Company of Toronto (one of the largest wholesale and retail coal distributing companies in Canada) should satisfy you as to the quality of this hard coal. This report was endorsed by many other Ontario coal dealers.
I shall read a few lines from this impressive Milnes' report, which has been widely published. I quote:
"I he results of these tests carried out in our own yards and the reports from our customers were remarkable. These reports convince us that this Alberta hard coal is practically smokeless and clean to handle and that it possesses all the burning qualities of high grade

American anthracite ... It is obviously of the greatest importance that large tonnages of this hard coal should be mined and delivered to the coal dealers of Ontario at the earliest possible moment. ... If a well designed plan for distribution is laid down to market a Canadian fuel of this quality at a reasonable price, we are confident that the product will soon command an extensive market throughout Ontario."
. Ladies and gentlemen-this property has continued to lie dormant in face of the fact that during the last 25 years we have sent out of Canada approximately $887,000,000 to purchase foreign anthracite.
And this is only part of the story.
According to consulting coal engineers of high repute-this hard coal can be mined and delivered to Ontario homes at from $12.50 to $13.25 per ton-after yielding a substantial profit. Yet the Ontario householder pays an average of $20 per ton for foreign hard coal of inferior quality. The Alberta hard coal would thus save him over $5 per ton-or $35 each year on seven tons-[DOT] an amount equal to another week's wages for the man in a low income bracket.
If 5,000,000 tons of this hard coal were shipped over our own railways-to the coal-less provinces of Ontario and Quebec-the saving would amount to $25,000,000 annually-an amount equal to four per cent interest on the whole funded debt of Ontario.
Ladies and gentlemen-a deposit of hundreds of millions oft tons of this high-grade hard coal lies dormant in Canada

while we depend upon foreign countries to supply us with this basic necessity of life.
Listen to the concluding paragraphs of a recent report on this Highwood coal property by one of the foremost consulting engineers of the United States:
"I am familiar with all the coal fields of western North America. I know of very large tonnages of low grade coal. But I know of no high grade coal deposit that has the physical characteristics of the Burns deposit.
In conclusion, I wish to emphasize several specific statements about the Burns coal. The quality of this high-grade coal has been amply demonstrated. It stands up well to sizing, handling, _ transportation and weather. It abounds in such thick beds under such apparently shallow cover that it can be strip-mined at low cost. It is the greatest known body of hard coal in -western North America and should command extensive -and profitable markets."
That indicates to what extent we could have developed Canada's natural resources to the end that we would have been supplying our own needs in superabundance. It can be shown conclusively that we are neglecting resources of equally remarkable richness and extent in respect of several other important needs of this nation. Any genuinely intelligent administration that set out- with the deliberate objective of making the Canadian people free and happy and prosperous would use these resources and would adopt the means that w'ould use them. That is just plain common sense. You do not have to have any Social Credit theories to see that that can be done. Social Credit would realize that these resources

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
ought to be developed and would take the measures that would develop them.
May I quote another statement on this matter of coal. I feel rather strongly about this question; the fact that Canada submits to huge yearly imports of coal is one of the main causes of the dollar shortage about which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is so much worried. What I cannot see is why the minister and his predecessors have not gone about some sort of solution of the problem, instead of simply getting up here and telling us about the trouble, while we go into debt and suffer. I quote from a submission to the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, of March 19, 1948, at page 4:
The Highwood hard coal contains an average of about 1,000 more B.T.U.'s or heat units per pound than the average pre-war American anthracite.
Inasmuch as probably 50 per cent of the coal in this extensive coal bearing area lies above valley or water level, competent consulting coal engineers have stated that this hard coal can be strip-mined and tunnel-mined at a very low cost per ton.
This hard coal can be mined-transported- and distributed in Ontario under existing mining costs and net freight rates at a price which will drastically lower home heating bills.
The annual solid fuel requirements of Ontario and Quebec for domestic heating approximate:
Ontario	
6,250,000	tonsQuebec	
2,250,000	tonsTotal	
8,500,000	tons
These total requirements are mainly met by United States coals and imported coke.
Limited tonnages of domestic coke are produced in Canada from American and Nova Scotia coal. A very limited tonnage of solid fuels fs' imported from overseas.
Between 1928 and 1940 Alberta shipped to Ontario an average of about 41,0:00 tons of coal annually, mainly to points in northern and western Ontario.
We submit that this large central Canada solid fuel requirement can be ultimately mainly supplied by the development of the Highwood hard coals in Alberta.
Attached to this general brief is a separate brief referring more specifically to the quantity and quality of coal in the Rio Alto (Burns) properties.
It is undoubtedly your desire that Canadian coal production be vastly increased in the shortest possible time-to conserve and obtain much needed American dollars.
It is undoubtedly your desire that if practicable, the standard of living be raised by drastically lowering home-heating costs.
Again and again, you have warned the people of the grave dangers that lie ahead in continuing to depend upon imports of foreign coal.
It is, we believe, your desire that the development of this Highwood area be carried out by individual initiative and private capital.
Given certain conditions, individual initiative and private capital wait the opportunity to develop the Highwood coal area with vigour and speed.
The essential condition is a firm understanding by one or both of the Canadian railway companies to construct a short spur line to serve the Highwood area.
This spur will be about 50 miles in length.
It should join the Canadian Pacific Calgary-McLeod branch line at Okotoks, Alberta.
This line from Okotoks to Calgary can easily carry another 5,000,000 tons or more of freight annually to the main line of the C.P.R. at Calgary and to the C.N.R. at the same point.
The total cost of this short rail spur line from Okotoks to the Highwood Coal areas should not exceed $1,500,000 inclusive of steel rails.
The grade should be about half of one per cent in favour of the load.
Construction will involve very little rock cutting and no large bridges have to be built.
The spur can be constructed in about four months. If done as a war measure or a greatly needed post-war project, it might be built even more quickly.
Whereas in pre-war periods a large amount of manual labour was required in rail construction, the job can now be accomplished largely by mechanical means, using bull-dozers, et cetera, with a great saving of manpower and capital.
It is strange to hear comment from time to time about the "immense task and cost" of building a fifty-mile rail spur to make the product of this vast coal area available to the people of Canada.
After that information has gone on record, Mr. Speaker, if the people of Ontario and Quebec do not rise in a united demand that their fuel interests shall be looked after by the government in power here, then I must say I stand absolutely amazed at the people of Ontario and Quebec.
I turn now from production, which is the first fundamental essential if we are to avoid inflation. What are the main monetary principles involved in Social Credit proposals? They are, first, a monetary authority which would have charge of all monetary affairs within the dominion. Second, the creation of debt-free money to be spent-not lent- into circulation. This debt-free money to be backed by the goods and services, producing and consuming, of the country. This principle is the centre and core of the whole series of Social Credit proposals. Third, the use of such money to stabilize the price structure. Fourth, the progressive elimination of the debt system of finance.
I said I would undertake to show that these principles are realistic, scientific and sound. As a beginning to keep my promise, may I refer to some men whose authority as financial students it will be hard to question. First I refer to Vincent C. Vickers, who was connected with the Vickers Company in Britain.
These are the things which help to establish the authority of Mr. Vickers. He was an Oxford graduate. Consequently, as an Oxford graduate he got a whole lot of unrealistic
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

ideas into his head which, when he finally got them out, proved beyond any shadow of doubt that he had discovered the weakness of the orthodox and the virtues of the new. He was deputy lieutenant of the city of London; a director of Vickers Limited for twenty-two years; a director of the Bank of England from 1910 to 1919; president of the Economic Reform Club and Institute, London.
He died in November, 1939. He wrote a book named "Economic Tribulation", and finished it almost on his dying bed. It was first published in 1941 and printed in Great Britain by Stephen Austin and Sons of Hertford. These facts concerning this man indicate that if he, in the circumstances under which he was raised and lived, and considering the society among which he moved, could change his opinion from the orthodox notions of finance to opinions similar to those of Social Credit, there is something or other in the Social Credit proposals that appeal to the mind of a thinker. Vincent C. Vickers advocated at the close of his book (1) a national monetary agency; (2) stabilization of price levels through the use of that agency; (3) debt-free money spent-not lent-into circulation; (4) the abolition of the debt system of finance. See how closely his recommendations follow the Social Credit idea. Here are some quotations from his book, from which hon. members can draw their own conclusions as to whether what I have said is true. At page 74 of "Economic Tribulation" we find:
1.	State control and state issue of currency and credit through a central organization managed and controlled by the state.
2.	Stabilization of the wholesale price level of commodities; that is to say, a fixed and constant internal purchasing power of money; so that a pound will buy tomorrow what it bought yesterday; an honest pound, not a fluctuating pound. And this can be done by so issuing and regulating the volume of available credit and currency that it shall at all times be adequate to permit of the purchasing power of the consumer being equated with the volume of production; not by limiting the purchasing power, but by firstly increasing purchasing power more in proportion to the productive capacity of industry.
4. Any additional supply of money should be issued as a clear asset to the state; so that money will be spent into existence, and not lent into existence.
7. The abolition of the debt system where all credit is created by the banks and hired out at interest to the country.
Mr. Speaker, as regards that stand of Mr. Vincent Vickers, taken after a lifetime of careful study of the economic tribulation in which he found the world, which resulted shortly after his death in the greatest war of all

time, the conclusions of such a man are surely such that they ought to be treated with respect.
May I turn to another eminent authority, whom I think hon. members will find equal difficulty in disregarding. I refer to Professor Paul H. Douglas of the University of Chicago's economics department. This man has written a book called "Controlling Depressions", published in 1935. Any hon. member who has not read that book with great care I would urge to read it with great care because it is of great value. If he reads it he will come away from it a much wiser man than when he approached it. I found it one of the most compelling books I ever read, most instructive and enlightening on every aspect of economics. This is what Professor Paul H. Douglas says, after a well-documented study of the whole field of economics in so far as he could compress it in a book of about 280 pages. This is taken from his conclusion on page 278:
A nationally managed system of currency and credit until such time as an international system may be perfected.
The removal from private banking of the power of creating commercial credit' and the lodging of this function in a socialized agency which will serve as the manufacturer and wholesaler of credit, and with private institutions serving merely as the retailers.
The creation of credit by this socialized agency should follow two main principles: (a) to provide, so far as possible, employment or useful work for those throwm out of their jobs by business depressions, and (b) to stabilize in a rough manner the general price level.
Hon. members will notice that his proposals generally do not conform so completely with the Social Credit concept as the proposals of Vincent Vickers; nevertheless there is a striking resemblance even there. Hon. members will be interested to find that Professor Douglas advocates dividends in certain circumstances.
I refer now to certain examples of debt-free money in history, cases in which debt-free money has been used with unquestionable success. I shall name a few: the Guernsey island experiment which commenced in 1815 and went to 1829, in which great quantities of money, considering the size of the island, were issued, apparently backed by the going-concern activities of the island, and were used in building a market house, paying for debts, building dikes, building schools and so on. No ill results were noticed. This experiment is thoroughly described in a book which hon. members will find in the library, called "An Example of Communal Currency", by J. Theodore Harris, published in 1911.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was the money finally redeemed?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A good deal of it was redeemed through collecting a fee on the market house after it was built, but a great deal of it remained in circulation.
Second, the greenback experiment through which Abraham Lincoln issued over $400 million of greenbacks, backed by goods and services, produced and consumed by the United States in his time, and won the civil war.
Third, Britain's Bradbury experiment, discussed fully in two books which are found in the library by Doctor William A. Shaw: the first, "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges", published in 1926, and the second, "The Theory and Principles of Central Banking", published in 1930. They are very revealing in their instructive consideration of this subject. With these books in the library, I stand amazed that so many hon. members in the house have never given any attention to the important matter of money and what can be done with money in the way of creating a new order, not money that is collected from the people but money that can be created by the state, backed by the goods produced by the state and used by the state by being spent into circulation to improve the general economic well-being of the nation.
Fourth, the $26,000,000 which Canada created during world war I, which was spent into circulation during that war, and which saved the interest that would have been charged on $26,000,000 of debt.
The thing which I have been utterly amazed at is that there was no money created during the recent war by the government, but every single cent of the cost of that war was saddled on the Canadian people as a debt to bear interest for an indefinite period of time. This constitutes one of the public crimes of the administration occupying the seats of government today.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I must remind the hon. member that his time is exhausted.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has about three minutes to go.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to burden the house, but may I discuss briefly one or two aspects of the Guernsey island experiment Which everybody finds interesting. There is a great writer on economics with whom everybody is more or less familiar. I refer to Sir Norman Angell. He published a little booklet, called "Your
Money," around 1936. It is an interesting little booklet. There are two statements made in the little volume to which I would direct the attention of hon. members, because they have a bearing on what we have just been discussing, the matter of the Guernsey island experiment. They 'help to show how it was that Guernsey island was able to issue the money *without causing inflation, and the extent to which she could have issued it without causing inflation. Sir Norman Angell says that the amount of money which a nation needs in circulation depends upon the number of exchanges of goods for goods, goods for services, services for goods which need to be effected in the nation; that every one of these exchanges requires money because money is the medium of exchange. Wherever an exchange is required there has to be the medium; therefore there has to be money. That gives us a valuable key to the amount of money which can safely be created in a state. I quote from the little booklet to which I referred. On page 31 the following appears:
Guernsey's method had obvious advantages, and speaking broadly, achieved its objects and was successful.
Again this statement:
It is not "backing" which of itself is the determining factor, but quantity in relation to exchanges needing to be operated.
I quote that because it gives such a useful hint as to the amount of money which can be created safely in a state and used without causing inflation,
I had other things which I thought I would say, Mr. Speaker, but I do not feel it is becoming that I should use the time of the house any further. Therefore I will leave other things to which I wished to refer, particularly quotations from Doctor William A. Shaw in those great books of his, and quotations from other eminent authorities, which I shall probably bring to the attention of the house at some future time.
May I now just lay down a conclusion Which I challenge anyone in this house to question and prove to be untrue. Social Credit proposals are realistic, scientific, and sound, and can be so established from the finest authorities to be found in the world today, as well as from experience; Social Credit proposals will not cause inflation.
I would urge upon hon. members once again, and upon the dominion government as a whole, that there lies hope for security in Canada and an abundance with freedom, only
The Budget-Mr. Boucher

through Social Credit, only through the use of the power which was given to Canada by the British North America Act to create currency and credit in accordance with public need. I commend Social Credit proposals as an alternative to this bleak and forbidding budget which we are now considering throughout Canada, and from which we shall at once commence to suffer.

speechtext: Who wants to die?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who wants to die in Canada, as my hon. friend says?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not under a good government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has been, in his own words, quite generous. In respect of those foodstuffs that were previously subject to the sales tax, he has given relief, and he says he will lose revenue that should go to the treasury to the extent of something like $20,000,000 in the year. There are about 12,000,000 Canadians, and the cancellation of this tax will mean on the average a saving of about $1.60 per person per annum. That is not a very generous gesture in the attempt to bring relief from the high cost of living and the heavy taxation which the people have to bear. It indicates to me that the government has had inculcated in its mind, as a result of wartime psychology, the idea that it must tax the Canadian people in order to keep them thrifty. It must save money for
Canadians because Canadians cannot be allowed to save for themselves. I believe the government has reflected its firm conviction that the Canadian people cannot be thrifty, cannot save for themselves without the assistance of the paternalistic front row in the House of Commons to do their saving for them-a paternalistic government represented in the person of the Minister of Finance.
To me that is an entirely false conception of the very spirit of Canadianism. We in this country are an aggressive people, willing to work, anxious to work, a thrifty people who are eager to put aside something for a rainy day without the government helping us to do so.
I believe that we have experienced in Canada much greater thrift on the part of the average citizen than we have on the part of the government in the matter of expenditures. I believe that if the government, in their budget, had announced where they were going to economize a little more on the reckless expenditures we have had, instead of saying they were going to make it so that people could not spend and could not buy scarce materials, the Canadian people would give a much better reception to the budget that is brought before us.
I think of the people with whom I come in contact daily; that is, the farming people in my community who are producing the goods for export and working eight, ten, twelve and eighteen hours a day to do so; these farmers are assisted by their wives and members of their families, all working on a joint venture for the production of much-needed goods to help out a hungry world. I am amazed when I find the government sending out to them an income tax statement and1 asking them to fill out that income tax form if they want to take advantage of the three-year average in taxation, asking them to fill out a long, white sheet, telling everything they are worth, their total assets; saying in this House of Commons: "You must have it understood that you do not have to do it until we demand you to do it", but continuing to send it out and asking them to do it, and having them believe they must do it; going to them through their representatives and saying: "You have not done so now, so we must do it. Show me your bank account for the last ten years; tell me what you have purchased for the last ten years, what you have given away for the last ten years, what you have built in the last ten years, by what amount you have inci'eased your assets in the last ten years." By such procedure you will undoubtedly arouse the resentment of anybody placed in that position.
The Budget-Mr. Boucher

It is not fair to agriculture, because agriculture will see what the government is doing for other classes of people. Immediately the farmer realizes that double depreciation has been given to industry to increase their plants, their machinery, to enlarge their capacity for production, to increase their manufacturing facilities by their capital investment at a rate, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Maedonnell) pointed out, seven times as great as that of the United States, there is every reason for him to feel dissatisfied with the requirements made upon him with regard to taxation.
Sometimes when I am out in my country and meet my farm constituents, they ask me if any of those in the front row have ever been on a farm; if they would like to come out and help make up their financial statement, their income statement for the last ten years; if they would like to help them calculate their increase in capital investment, their depreciation, their basic earnings, their three-year earnings; how they could decide that, where the daughter has lived for twenty-seven, twenty-eight or thirty years at home on the farm, helped the housewife in the house, driven the horse on the hayfork, driven the hayrake out in the field, raised the poultry to pay for the groceries of the house, raised pigs to pay for the taxes for the year, yet the farmer would not be allowed, as an exemption, her wages because the main work was within the house. Then there is the young fellow under twenty-one years of age, learning his trade of farming, perhaps attending school, going home from school and doing as many of us who have been brought up on the farm have done, taking off his school clothes and getting into his overalls, doing chores until eight or nine o'clock at night, and then going in to do his homework. Those in that position cannot help reflecting on the difference between such and those who are not in pursuit of agriculture.
I think a great picture can be painted -that would impel this government in reason to allow consideration not only to the farmer who works many more hours than seven or eight a day, five or six or seven days a week, and to give more just compensation to individual initiative in the production of much needed goods commensurate with the work done, and the application given in that regard.
The same thing could be said about the smaller business people. When the small businessman or the young man setting up in a small business-be it a garage, a store, a workshop or any artisan trade-can see a big manufacturing company, as has been the case, allowed to increase its capital investment [DOT]with double depreciation, while he is not allowed to do so, you again force that man to believe that this House of Commons is catering to big interests and, irrespective of what are the demands of the present day, is not considering the needs of the smaller man.
Then, when you see within our cities the civil servant, the man who is employed by the government, getting the great promises he did a year or so ago, of a re-examination of civil service salaries, wages, living conditions and classifications; when you see the Gordon report recommend that certain department offices be taken from the operation of the Civil Service Act and the appointments left to the treasury board or to a committee of the cabinet; then, when you find out that, after all that is done, the charwoman in the House of Commons can come to work about 4.30 or 5 o'clock in the morning, trudging here from -her home which may be at some distance, work until about 9.30 in the morning and get a mere $3 or $4 a day, while you find the private secretary to the Prime Minister of Canada receiving a raise in pay per year of $5,000, you will find that there is plenty of reason for discontentment and dissatisfaction, and a demand for a better deal.
It is now eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I do not intend to proceed with my discussion of this matter tonight. I feel that it is but my duty, however, to point out, as critically as I can, the total lack of a realistic approach to the problems of the day in the budget as announced. I believe that the Canadian people would produce more, would be happier and would in a much greater measure solve our problems of high prices, high taxation and United States dollars if the government showed more confidence in their ability to do so than the budget reflects.
In conclusion, may I say that I believe, if our Canadian farmer were allowed to export his meat products and his farm production to the United States and sell them at the price he could receive for them there, without export restrictions, it would give us more United States dollars than the Minister of Finance is able to tell us that his austerity program has brought in since its inception.
On motion of Mr. McKay, the debate was adjourned.
